activity: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
knowledge_domain: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
fact: In many parliamentary systems, a government that loses a vote of no confidence in the lower house must resign or call a general election.
story:
The television in the corner of the student common room was tuned to a news channel nobody had chosen, and by the time Kayla noticed it, the vote was already underway. Rows of legislators, an electronic tally board, a speaker's voice clipped by the room's bad acoustics. She had come in to find Ayva, who owed her a highlighter and half a sheet of notes on the comparative politics unit, and instead she stood still, bag sliding off her shoulder, watching the numbers climb.

"Is that a no confidence vote?" Arthur asked from the couch, chin propped on his fist. He was the sort of person who watched parliamentary channels for entertainment, which Kayla had always found faintly anachronistic in someone their age, like collecting vinyl or writing letters.

"So what happens if they lose?" she asked. "Does the prime minister just stay anyway?"

Arthur shook his head without looking away from the screen. "In a lot of parliamentary systems, if the government loses that vote in the lower house, it has to resign or call a general election."

The tally finished. The government had lost. On screen, the prime minister gathered her papers with an unhurried, almost clerical calm, and Kayla felt something rearrange itself in her understanding, quietly and without permission. She had spent two evenings on Mr. Levy's essay prompt, trying to compare how a parliamentary system and a presidential one choose and remove a head of government, and she had been circling the same paragraph like water around a drain. In the presidential system she knew best, the president served a fixed term, removable only through a cumbersome process nobody ever finished. Here, on this screen, a majority of one house had just ended a government in an afternoon. She kept thinking about the papers. The prime minister had gathered them as if tidying a desk at the end of a workday.

Mr. Levy had assigned the essay the week before, on a Tuesday she could still recall with the sting of an unfinished argument. He had said, leaning against the whiteboard, that he wanted positions, not encyclopedias. "Tell me which system you'd trust more," he had said, "and then tell me what you're still unsure about." That last instruction had annoyed her. She preferred questions with ends, and he had built the ambiguity in like a fault line. When she'd complained to Ayva afterward, Ayva had shrugged and said that uncertainty was just where you stood before you decided to pretend. Kayla hadn't spoken to her for the rest of lunch, though she'd known, even then, that Ayva was partly right.

She found Ayva at the far table now, highlighter already surrendered, and sat down across from her without preamble. "I think I've got it," Kayla said. "The essay. I was writing about removal like it was a punishment, a thing that happens when somebody breaks something. But in a parliamentary system, it's more like a test that's always running. The government only exists because the lower house lets it." She turned her notebook sideways so Ayva could see the two columns she'd drawn, arrows running in opposite directions. "The president gets chosen separately from the legislature, so the legislature can't just withdraw support. The prime minister comes out of the parliament itself."

"So which do you trust?" Ayva asked, uncapping the highlighter with her teeth.

"That's where I keep getting stuck." Kayla looked back toward the television, where the anchors had begun to excoriate the fallen government, calling its final months a catalogue of evasion, and a dissident member of the old ruling party was already giving interviews about renewal. Speed, she thought, was the obvious argument: a government that had lost the house's confidence could be replaced at once, no long twilight, no leader governing for years without a majority. But speed in both directions could be a trap, too. A government that could fall in an afternoon could also be kept hostage to an afternoon's mood. She said as much, haltingly, watching Ayva's pen hover over the notes without writing anything down.

"Then write it that way," Ayva said. "Say you can't tell. Levy said he wanted the unsure part."

"I know what he said. It's just not how I like to end things."

That evening, in her room with the lamp on and the essay open, Kayla read her own two columns again. She thought about the prime minister gathering her papers, about how much power can leave a person without ceremony, and she thought about a president she remembered watching on television years ago, still in office, still speaking, while half the country demanded his removal and the machinery ground nowhere. Both were true at once. She wrote her position in one paragraph and her uncertainty in the next, and when she got to the end of the uncertain paragraph she let it sit, ragged and unfinished, instead of sanding it down. Then she saved the file, closed the laptop, and looked out the window at the streetlamp blinking on below.

activity: to argue both sides of a Supreme Court case about free speech before a mock court
knowledge_domain: to argue both sides of a Supreme Court case about free speech before a mock court
fact: In West Virginia v. Barnette (1943), the Supreme Court ruled 6-3 that public schools cannot force students to salute the flag or recite the Pledge of Allegiance.
story:
The courthouse hallway smelled of floor wax and old paper, and Amelia kept her notes against her chest like a shield while Ms. Balogun arranged the students into order outside the borrowed courtroom. Amelia had drawn the Respondents, which meant she would defend the school district's right to compel the flag salute, and she had spent two weeks learning to believe it. That was the assignment: argue both sides, one today and one next week, and be graded on whether you could make the weaker position sound like a position at all.

The problem was that she already knew how the real case had ended. On the drive over, Emie had leaned across the seat, phone out, and read aloud from a summary. "West Virginia v. Barnette, 1943," Emie said. "The Supreme Court ruled six to three that public schools cannot force students to salute the flag or recite the Pledge of Allegiance." She said it the way you'd recite a score, and then she asked, "So why do we still have to stand in homeroom? Like, can they actually make us?" Amelia hadn't answered, because the question had a shape she couldn't close, like a shoebox with the lid bent.

Inside, the courtroom was real in a way their classroom never was: the judge's bench towering, the flag in its corner, a bailiff who had better things to do. Christine was presiding, having won the honor by coin toss, and she had already stacked her papers into a gavel-shaped tower. Ms. Balogun sat in the second row with a legal pad and the expression of someone prepared to be surprised.

Amelia stood at the podium and began. Compulsory salute, she argued, was not censorship; the state compelled conduct, not belief. No student was required to proselytize for any creed; they were required only to participate in a civic ritual that held a fractured country together during a war. She heard her own voice go flat in places where her convictions weren't, and louder in the places where they unexpectedly were. She had found, reading the old briefs at her kitchen table, that the compelled-salute argument wasn't simply obedience dressed up. There was a real fear underneath it, a fear that a democracy could dissolve if its symbols were optional. She didn't think the fear justified the rule. But she could no longer call it stupid.

Then the student judges questioned her, and a boy on the panel, one of the quieter ones, asked whether the school could force a student to say the Pledge aloud, word for word. Amelia opened her mouth to maneuver and stopped. "No," she said. "They can't. In 1943 the Supreme Court ruled six to three that public schools cannot force students to salute the flag or recite the Pledge of Allegiance. West Virginia v. Barnette." She felt the room shift, felt Ms. Balogun's pen stop. "So my argument isn't that the law permits it. My argument is why the Court might have been wrong to say it doesn't."

She finished, sat down, and watched her opposing counsel, a senior named only on the roster as Second Chair, dismantle her in four minutes with Barnette held up like a lantern. It was over quickly. The exhilaration Amelia had expected to feel at the end was there, but tangled with something more like vertigo, because her best moment had been the moment she'd argued against herself.

Afterward Emie found her by the water fountain. "You tanked your own case," Emie said, not accusing, more curious. Amelia wiped her mouth with the back of her hand. "I didn't tank it. I located it." That sounded pretentious and she let it stand. "Next week I argue the families. The kids who wouldn't salute." Emie tilted her head. "So which side do you actually believe?" Amelia thought about the shoebox question from the car, whether standing in homeroom was compelled speech or just tired courtesy, whether it mattered that the ones refusing were mostly doing it for reasons she admired and a few for reasons she didn't. She didn't know yet, and she suspected the honest brief was the one that admitted it.

Ms. Balogun came down the aisle collecting papers. "Ms. Reyes," she said, which was Second Chair, and then, catching Amelia's eye, "and you. Both of you, next week, be prepared to lose the argument you love." It wasn't kindness exactly, but it wasn't a reprimand either.

On the courthouse steps the air had turned warm, and Emie was already scrolling for a bus schedule. Amelia held her notes at her side now, not against her chest, and read the top page of the opposing brief she'd written for the families, the one where she'd typed a sentence she'd since crossed out and then uncrossed: that some principles feel axiomatic only until you have to defend them, and that the defense is worth doing anyway. She folded the page in half and put it in her back pocket.

"Do you think," Emie said, squinting up at the courthouse flag, "if I just sit down during the pledge tomorrow, I get detention?" Amelia zipped her bag. "Only one way to find out."

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: Food-safety guidance says refrigerated food must be kept at or below 4 degrees Celsius (40 degrees Fahrenheit) to slow the growth of bacteria.
story:
The sign at the church hall door said Neighborhood Cleanup and Food Drive, and beneath it, in smaller letters, Sort Room Volunteers Enter Here. Taylor had signed up because Mary had signed up, and Mary had signed up because college applications wanted evidence of character, though neither of them said that out loud. Inside, the sort room smelled of cardboard and bananas. Ms. Mokoena, who ran the food bank on Saturdays, handed them clipboards and pointed to a wall chart of categories: canned protein, grains, baby formula, refrigerated.

"Refrigerated?" Taylor said. She hadn't thought of a food bank having a cold aisle.

"Whole cooler in the back," Ms. Mokoena said. "Come find me if anything seems off." Then she was gone toward the loading dock, where Haydn was wrestling a dolly of mixed donations through the propped door.

The morning took shape around small decisions. Dented cans, yes or no. Expired crackers, yes or no. Taylor liked the sorting; it felt like each box held a little argument about what still counted as food. Haydn, working beside her, liked to expatiate on every judgment call, holding up a jar of marmalade and delivering a two-minute lecture on how marmalade was underappreciated, until Mary told him to just put it in the grains pile and stop narrating.

The problem arrived with the milk. Haydn wheeled in a crate of gallon jugs, plastic fogged with sweat, and set it down beside the door while he went back for the next load. Taylor touched one of the jugs without thinking, the way you'd test a kettle, and it was warm. Not hot. Just the temperature of the room, which was the temperature of the June morning outside. She stood with her hand on the plastic and wondered how long warm had to last before it became something else. Did the clock start at the dock? At the donor's fridge? She had never once considered that milk had a clock at all.

"Those can't sit here," Mary said, coming back from the break room. She'd done this before, last summer, and Taylor had noticed her checking a thermometer taped to the cooler door earlier, squinting at it like it was a test question. "Refrigerated food has to be kept at or below four degrees Celsius," Mary said. "Four degrees Celsius, forty degrees Fahrenheit. That's the line." She said it flatly, a rule she'd memorized, and Taylor noticed she said it twice a shift, apparently, to anyone near a crate.

Taylor looked at the jug in her hand, then at the cooler across the room, then at the loading dock where the rest of the milk still stood in the sun. The rule was simple. The situation wasn't. The donations had come from a grocery drive at the elementary school; some teacher had clearly asked families to give what they could, and somebody's family had given milk, probably from their own fridge that morning, probably meaning it kindly. If Taylor followed the rule, six gallons went into the bin and that family's kindness went with it. If she broke the rule, somebody's kid drank questionable milk on Tuesday. She turned the jug over, looking for a time stamp, and found only a sell-by date that told her nothing about today.

"What do we do," she asked Mary, "if we don't know how long it's been warm?"

Ms. Mokoena appeared in the doorway before Mary could answer, reading the room the way adults who run volunteer operations learn to. She didn't lecture. She asked Taylor what she thought, and Taylor heard herself laying out two positions she hadn't known she held until she said them. One was the strict one: a rule exists because nobody at the point of decision can know the history of the jug, so you follow the rule and the cost is six gallons, which the food bank could replace with a check to the dairy shelf. The other was the humane one: the whole point of a food bank is that hunger doesn't get to be careful, and there was something almost ascetic about tossing good intentions into the bin to keep a chart clean. Taylor surprised herself by naming the first position utilitarianism, a word from Mr. Whatever's ethics unit that she'd never expected to use out loud, and Mary laughed and said, "Look at you," and Taylor felt her ears go warm.

"I don't know which one wins," Taylor admitted. "Maybe neither. Maybe the answer is that we ask people to donate shelf-stable milk next time, and today we follow the rule, and I still feel bad about it."

Ms. Mokoena considered that for a moment, then said, "Then write that on the sign-up sheet for the fall drive. The feeling bad part is called learning the job." She picked up a jug herself, weighed it in one hand like a small decision, and carried it to the bin.

Taylor grabbed two more. On the loading dock, in the sun, the rest of the crate waited, and she went out to get it.

activity: graduating from high school
knowledge_domain: graduating from high school
fact: The square graduation cap is called a mortarboard because it resembles the flat board bricklayers use to hold mortar.
story:
The cap had been fighting Jack all afternoon, and by the time they reached the restaurant it had won twice, once in the parking lot and once at the crosswalk, where a gust sent it spinning into the gutter and Foster had to chase it past a parked Honda. Jack carried it now under his arm like a reluctant pet, its tangle of tassel swinging against his ribs.

They had gotten a booth by the window, which Massimo declared a strategic victory, and the waitress had looked at their gowns bunched on the bench seat and said, "Big night, huh," in the flat tone of someone who had served eleven years of graduation dinners and been desensitized by all of them. She set down four waters without asking whether they wanted anything else.

"Four?" Jack said. He'd counted three of them.

"Ms. Gallagher's coming," Massimo said. "I ran into her outside the auditorium. She said she wanted to buy the graduating class a slice of pie, and I said fine, but only if it's the class represented by me and these two."

"That's not what I said," Foster said. "I said the whole class, minus everyone we don't like."

"Which is the same three people," Massimo said. "It's set theory."

Jack put the cap on the table between the salt and the ketchup and studied it. He had worn the thing for three hours and still did not understand its design. It was a flat square perched on a skull-shaped fitted base, and the two shapes agreed with each other the way a hat agrees with an octopus. Every time he turned his head the board tipped; every time the wind picked up it tried to leave.

"Why is it like this?" he said. "Seriously. Somebody chose this shape. Somebody made a decision."

"Tradition," Foster said, in the voice he used for words that meant shut up.

"Tradition isn't a reason. Somebody drew this on paper and other people nodded."

Ms. Gallagher arrived before anyone could murder the topic. She sat down, confiscated a menu, and said she'd been grading senior portfolios all week and wanted to look at people who weren't asking for extensions. When the waitress came back, Jack pointed at the cap and asked her, because he was testing whether anyone in the world knew.

She didn't. Massimo guessed it was so you could see people in a crowd, which explained nothing. Foster guessed nuns. It was Ms. Gallagher who leaned in, tapped the flat board once with her finger, and said, "It's called a mortarboard." Then she leaned back and drank her water and offered nothing further, because she was the kind of teacher who considered a fact delivered and a fact explained to be two very different crimes.

Jack turned it over. The board, the flat square. "Mortar," he said slowly. "Like bricklayers. They hold the mortar on a flat board."

"Close," Ms. Gallagher said, which was as close as she came to applause. Massimo picked the cap up and balanced it flat on his palm, a little gray square platform, and everyone at the table looked at it with the mild astonishment of people discovering that an object they'd resented for years had a history. "So we're all dressed as bricklayers," Foster said. "Great. I spent forty dollars on a tassel to dress as a guy with a trowel."

The melancholic part, Jack decided, was not the cap. The melancholic part was that in September he would be in a city where nobody knew him, and Massimo would be two states away studying something he called applied mathematics and everyone else called showing off, and Foster would be taking a gap year he described as "figuring it out," which Jack suspected meant working at the garden center and thinking about it. Ms. Gallagher would get a new crop of seniors, and by October she would have trouble remembering all their names, and that was not a flaw in her, it was just how time worked on people. The mortarboard, on the other hand, had been his nemesis all afternoon and he now found he almost liked it. A hat that made you look like a mason. Something built, going on top of something being built. He could live with that as a metaphor, though he suspected the metaphor was mostly luck.

"So what's the plan?" Massimo said, mouth full of pie. "For the fall. You never say."

"I don't have a speech," Jack said. "I'm going, and I'm going to figure out the rest there, and I'm going to be honest that I haven't figured it out here."

"That's the saddest plan I've ever heard."

"It's a load-bearing plan," Jack said, and put the cap back on his head, squared it, and pushed open the door into the wind.

activity: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
knowledge_domain: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
fact: Capitalization means unpaid interest is added to a loan's principal, so from then on interest is charged on the interest too.
story:
Zachary counted the drawer for the third time and came up two dollars short, which meant the register had eaten a toonie again, and Mr. Do would make his slow, patient peroration about care and attention before letting him go home. It was Friday night at the hardware store, the hour when the lights hummed and nobody came in except people with plumbing emergencies. Zachary didn't mind the quiet. He minded the two dollars.

His brother had called at lunch, before the shift started, and the call was still sitting in his stomach like a swallowed stone. Zachary had heard the whole thing while pretending to eat his sandwich: the loan statement, the number on it, the number being bigger than what his brother had actually borrowed. Four years of school, and somehow the balance had grown while he wasn't looking. "I haven't even missed a payment," his brother kept saying, "I'm on the plan where you don't pay yet," and then the line had gone quiet in the way it does when someone is reading the statement again.

At seven, Carlo came through the door in his delivery jacket, ostensibly to buy furnace filters, actually to talk. Carlo wanted a synthesizer, a used one he'd found online for three hundred and eighty dollars, and he'd been transferring ten dollars a week into a savings account since September. "The lady at the bank said it earns interest," Carlo said, leaning on the counter near the rubber mallets. "Like, they pay me for keeping it there. Two percent, whatever that means. It's like four cents a month, but it's mine."

"Four cents a month," Zachary said.

"Don't mock the four cents. The four cents compounds."

Zachary rang up the filters and thought about his brother. Interest on savings, growing because you left it alone. Interest on a loan, growing whether you paid it or not. He had understood, before Friday, that interest was what you paid for borrowing, but he had imagined it as something flat, a fee, finished once it was charged. Somewhere between the lunch call and Carlo's four cents, the floor of that idea gave way. If interest could sit on savings and make more interest, it could sit on a loan and do the same thing.

"Hey," Zachary said. "You know anything about student loans?"

Carlo shrugged. "Olivia's sister has one. She calls it the thing that never sleeps."

When Olivia came in at closing to buy batteries, as she did every Friday because her flashlight died every Thursday, Zachary asked her outright, and Olivia texted her sister right there among the duct tape. The answer came back in screenshot form, a paragraph from the loan website, and Zachary read it twice under the checkout light. Unpaid interest added to the principal, so from then on interest was charged on the interest too. The word for it was in bold. He said it out loud without meaning to.

"Capitalization," Carlo read over his shoulder. "Sounds like a crime."

"It kind of is one," Zachary said. "It's why his balance is bigger than what he borrowed. He didn't pay the interest while he was in school, so they folded it into the loan, and now the interest charges interest. Meanwhile your four cents does the same thing in reverse."

Olivia held up her phone. "My sister says to open a savings account before you graduate and never look at it. She says look at the loan, don't look at the savings. That's her whole advice. She also says hi."

Mr. Do emerged from the back with the deposit bag and his air of perspicacious calm, the air of a man who had watched three decades of teenagers make the same discoveries he had already made. He didn't lecture them. He only said, "Lights out in five," and stood by the door while Zachary finished counting.

Walking home under the parking lot glare, Zachary called his brother back. He didn't have a plan, exactly; he had a word, and a picture of a number that had been quietly feeding itself, and a second picture, Carlo's four cents doing the same trick on the other side of the ledger. "You could pay the interest part before it capitalizes," he said. "Even small amounts. I looked it up on break." There was a pause on the line, and then the sound of his brother pulling up the statement on a laptop, keys clicking somewhere far away in a rented room.

"Show me the numbers," his brother said. "Read them to me again."

activity: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
knowledge_domain: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
fact: In France, the directly elected president appoints the prime minister, but the National Assembly can force the prime minister's government to resign by passing a censure motion.
story:
Rose had claimed the corner table by the microfiche cabinets an hour ago, and now three books on comparative government stood open around her like witnesses. The assignment was due Thursday: compare how a parliamentary system and a presidential system each choose and remove a head of government. She had understood the simple versions by tenth grade. Parliament picks a prime minister from the winning party, and parliament can bring that government down. A president is elected separately and serves a fixed term no legislature can touch. The trouble was that she had stopped there, and Mr. Do, who taught the politics elective, had written "so which is better?" at the bottom of her outline in his cramped red hand, as if the question were answerable.

She turned to Caleigh, who had spread her own notes across the other half of the table. "Okay, so here's my problem," Rose said. "In Canada the parliament can force out the prime minister basically whenever it loses confidence. In the States, Congress can't remove the president except through impeachment, which almost never works. I have two systems and no way to say anything interesting about them."

"That's not a problem, that's the whole essay," Caleigh said, without looking up. She was the sort of student who could beseech a deadline into moving and somehow the deadline would move. "Just say the fixed term protects stability and the confidence thing protects accountability."

Rose wanted that to be enough. She wrote it down, read it back, and felt the flatness of it, a sentence that could close a door. Last year she had written a whole essay on electoral reform the same way, tidy and empty, and Mr. Do had given her an A with a note that said "competent, careful, safe," and she had stared at the word safe for a long time afterward, deciding whether it was praise. She hadn't decided yet.

Zayne arrived with a coffee he wasn't supposed to have in the library and dropped into the chair beside her. "You're still on that government thing?" He leaned over her outline. "My cousin lived in France for two years. She used to complain about it constantly. Half the time the president ran everything, half the time she said the parliament was bullying the government out of office."

Rose sat forward. "Bullying how?"

"Like, the government would just have to resign. It was a whole thing, some vote." He shrugged. "A censure motion, she called it. She said the Assembly passed one and the government fell."

Rose pulled the France volume toward her and started reading, one finger tracing the column. There it was, plain as plumbing: in France, the president was elected directly by the voters, and that president appointed the prime minister. But the National Assembly could force the prime minister's government to resign by passing a censure motion. She read it twice to be sure she had the direction right, because for a moment it seemed impossible that a prime minister chosen by a president could still be answerable to a parliament.

"That's not one system," she said slowly. "That's both. The head of state is elected like a president. The head of government can be brought down like a prime minister."

Caleigh looked up at last. "So France just cheats, and you can't use it."

"Or it's the counterpoint to my whole essay." Rose was already flipping to the index, looking for anything else the book would admit. "My two categories are pretending to be the only two categories. France mixes them, which means the choice isn't between stability and accountability, it's about where you put each one."

Zayne sipped his coffee. "I have no idea what that means, but it sounds better than what you had."

"It might also be wrong," Rose said. "Or half right. I don't know enough yet to say what the mixing costs." She thought of Mr. Do's red question again, so which is better, and felt the honest answer forming: better at what, for whom, decided by which voters in which decade. She wrote at the top of a clean page, "France: presidential choice of PM, parliamentary removal," and underlined it twice.

The library lights dimmed for the evening schedule, and the cashier from the little coffee cart began stacking chairs somewhere near the entrance. Caleigh packed her notes into her bag, querulous about the closing hour, saying she'd only just gotten comfortable. Rose stayed where she was, copying the citation, checking the page number twice, because she had gotten facts wrong before and remembered the specific heat of it, a presentation on bicameralism in eleventh grade where she had swapped the two houses and Zayne, of all people, had caught it from the back row.

"Walk out with me or stay?" Caleigh asked, shoulder bag on.

"Stay. Ten more minutes."

Caleigh left. Zayne lingered, reading the underlined sentence upside down, then said, "France, huh. So if the Assembly hates the prime minister, they can force the whole government out, even though the president picked him?"

"Even though the whole country picked the president," Rose said. "That's the part I can't stop looking at."

activity: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
knowledge_domain: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
fact: Raising the temperature speeds up both the forward and reverse reactions, but it speeds up the endothermic direction more, which is why the equilibrium shifts that way.
story:
Grandmother's kitchen smelled of vinegar and burnt sugar, which was, as far as Nevaeh could tell, the whole house's personality condensed into two ingredients. She had commandeered the table by the window, pushing aside a jigsaw puzzle of a lighthouse to make room for her chemistry notes, two sealed tubes of reddish gas Mr. Oyelaran had lent her from the supply cabinet, and a saucepan she was not technically supposed to touch.

The exam was Monday. Equilibrium, Le Chatelier's principle, forty multiple-choice questions and one free response that would decide whether she kept her scholarship average intact. She had a text from Frances open on the table: why doesn't heat just speed everything up equally?? it said, followed by three question marks, which in Frances's typography was a scream. Nevaeh did not have an answer, which was the problem. She'd read the textbook page twice and it kept saying the same thing in the same voice, like a receipt for information she hadn't actually bought.

She filled the saucepan with hot water from the tap and set it on the stove, then dug a bag of frozen peas from the freezer and laid it on a folded towel. The tubes went one in each. Brown gas in the warm one, she knew that much. She wanted to see it happen rather than take its word.

Her grandmother came through with a basket of laundry on her hip, looked at the pan, and looked at Nevaeh. "You cooking or doing science?"

"Science."

"In my good pan."

"It's just water, Grandma." The grandmother adjusted the flame anyway, lower, out of what Nevaeh recognized as principle rather than concern, and carried the basket toward the bedrooms. A minute later the phone buzzed again. Jerome: my dad says heat makes everything faster so the tube should just be more of whatever it is. Nevaeh typed back, that's what I thought too, and stopped, because it was what she'd thought too, and the tube in the warm water was getting darker, visibly, while the one under the peas was fading toward pale.

She sat with her chin on her hand and watched the warm tube darken. If heat sped up both directions equally, the mixture wouldn't change at all; it would just get there faster, the same balance arriving sooner. But the color was moving, which meant the balance itself was moving. So both reactions were being pushed, and one of them was being pushed harder. She pulled her notebook closer and wrote it out, half to herself, half for Frances: heat speeds up forward and reverse, but it speeds up the endothermic direction more. That was the whole trick. That was why the shift happened at all, and why the exam question made sense instead of being arbitrary. The word endothermic she'd been mispronouncing in her head all week; now she said it out loud to the empty kitchen, once, carefully, the way you test a floorboard.

The phone buzzed. Frances: wait so it's like the heat is playing favorites?? Nevaeh typed, basically, and then, thinking of Mr. Oyelaran saying the tube was a synecdoche for the whole unit, one small system standing in for every reversible reaction in the universe, she added, kind of. He'd used the word at the end of class on Friday and half the room had written it down wrong. She hadn't written it down at all; she'd just remembered it, which she suspected was worse.

The peas-tube had gone almost colorless now. She lifted it with the towel and held it beside the dark one, side by side, two states of the same stuff, and felt the small pugnacious satisfaction of a question that had refused to stay abstract and lost. Her grandmother came back through, paused at the table, and tapped the pale tube with one finger.

"That one's cold," her grandmother said.

"It's a reaction, Grandma. Shifting."

"Looks like nothing to me."

"That's sort of the point." Nevaeh took a photo of the two tubes and sent it to the group chat, then set the phone face down and copied her note into Frances's question as a reply: raising the temperature speeds up both the forward and reverse reactions, but it speeds up the endothermic direction more, which is why the equilibrium shifts that way. She read it over once. It still felt like a receipt, honestly, but this time she'd watched the purchase happen. There was a thing she couldn't explain, why heat preferred one direction at all, and she underlined the more in her notebook and left the why blank, on purpose, a small door she could come back through.

She turned off the burner, poured the water into the sink, and set both tubes on the windowsill where the light came through them, one amber, one clear, side by side. From the hallway her grandmother called that dinner was in an hour and that the puzzle pieces had better be back in their box. Nevaeh swept the lighthouse fragments into a pile with the side of her hand, then picked up the pale tube again and held it against her palm to warm it, watching the color gather back from the bottom like weather rolling in.

activity: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
knowledge_domain: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
fact: Le Chatelier's principle states that when a system at equilibrium is disturbed, the equilibrium shifts in the direction that partly counteracts the change.
story:
The bet was Brenna's idea, which meant it was already rigged in some way Jackson couldn't see yet. She had two sealed tubes of solution on the lab bench, both the same exhausted pink, and she was spinning one of them like a tiny glass baton. "Fifty cents," she said. "You heat that one, tell me first whether it gets pinker or bluer. Commit before the hot water bath."

Jackson leaned over the tube. Cobalt chloride, Ms. Koné had said at the start of the period, in a reaction sitting at equilibrium, which Jackson had privately translated as a reaction that had given up and decided to be two things at once. He knew heat was a disturbance. He knew, in the vernacular of the unit they were three days into, that a system at equilibrium that gets disturbed will shift in the direction that partly counteracts the change. The teacher had made them chant the last part. Partly, she'd said, tapping the board like it owed her money. Not entirely. The system tries to undo you, and it only half manages.

"Bluer," he said. "Heat it, it goes blue." It was a guess dressed up as a conclusion, but he'd been trying all week to seem like someone who knew things before he knew them, mostly because Brenna did, and Zoe kept score.

"Interesting," said Zoe, from the stool where she was supposed to be writing up her titration. "Wrong, but interesting." She held up a finger. "Wait, no. I don't know if it's wrong. I just like saying that."

"You're supposed to be neutral," Jackson said. "Like a Switzerland of fifty-cent wagers."

"Switzerland charges fees," Zoe said, and went back to her titration with the serene cruelty of someone who has already decided the outcome and is waiting for the universe to catch up.

Brenna lowered the tube into the hot water bath and they watched it like it was an egg about to hatch. Within seconds the pink began to transfigure itself, but not the way Jackson had called. The colour deepened toward purple, toward violet, toward a blue so stubborn it looked offended. Brenna fished the tube out with tongs and set it in the rack, glowing like a small neon argument. "Pink to blue," she said. "You said bluer. Is bluer the same as blue when the thing was pink? Because in the ordinary meaning of words, Jackson, you nailed it."

"That's exactly what I said." He picked up the tube, still warm, and turned it in the light. The thing that bothered him wasn't the fifty cents, which Zoe was already collecting from Brenna on the grounds that "bluer" was a coward's word for a coin flip. What bothered him was that he had said blue for no reason, and been right, and would not be right tomorrow when the reason mattered. He got his notebook and wrote: equilibrium, disturbed, shifts to partly counteract. Heated it, and it went blue. So the blue side had to be the side that fought back against heat, and if he cooled it now, the system would lean the other way, back toward pink, trying again to undo him.

"Give me the cold bath," he said, already reaching for the ice bucket, and Brenna moved the rack out of his range with one finger.

"Betting's closed," she said. "You already won once by accident, and once per day is the house limit."

"It's not a bet." He took the ice bucket anyway. "Le Chatelier's principle," he said, mostly to himself, because Ms. Koné had written the name on the board in green pen and he liked the weight of it, like a spell or a chess move. "You push, it pushes back partway. So I push cold, it should..." He trailed off, because here was the honest part, the part he wasn't going to say out loud: he didn't know how far partway went. The shift counteracted the change, it didn't erase it, which meant the tube in the ice would land somewhere new, not back where it started, and he couldn't predict the somewhere, only the direction. He slid the tube into the ice water and crouched until his eyes were level with the bench.

Zoe abandoned her titration and crouched beside him. Brenna crouched on his other side, chin on her fists, watching the blue like it might do something embarrassing if they blinked. Slowly, at the bottom of the tube, the first incipient threads of pink began to work their way up through the colour, faint as breath on a cold window, and none of them said anything at all.

activity: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
knowledge_domain: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
fact: A zero derivative does not guarantee a maximum or minimum: f(x) = x cubed has derivative zero at x = 0, but its graph keeps rising through that point.
story:
The corner store on Fenwick smelled of newspaper ink and the sweet syrup of the slushie machine, and Maelie had claimed the table by the window because it was the only one with a wobbly leg she could steady with her knee. She spread her notes across it: the practice exam, the derivative rules, the graph paper she had bought that morning with the last of her birthday money. The test was Monday. It was Friday, ten past nine, and the store closed at eleven.

"Show me the one you keep erasing," Dominic said. He set down two coffees and slid into the chair across from her, popping the lid off his despite the heat.

She turned the page toward him. "Revenue function. R of x. I took the derivative, set it equal to zero, solved for x, and that's the maximum. Four hundred units. Done."

"That's it?"

"That's it. That's the whole method."

Dominic pulled the sheet closer and read it without touching it, the way he read everything, as if the paper might accuse him later. "You didn't graph it."

"Why would I graph it? The derivative is zero there. Zero derivative, maximum. That's what the book says."

Ms. Papadopoulos, who owned the store and had let them use the table since September on the condition that they bought something every hour, came by with a cloth and wiped down the counter beside them. She said nothing, but she had a way of lingering that Maelie had learned to hear as an offer. Maelie ignored it. She was tired, and the method worked, and Dominic had a habit of complicating things that already worked.

"Plot a few points," he said. "Just points. Nothing fancy."

"Dom."

"Humor me. You've got the graph paper right there."

She took the pencil and marked points, annoyed at the waste of them, at the hour, at the way the eraser had already grayed the sheet. Then she marked the point where her derivative was zero, and she sat back, and something in the shape did not close the way she expected it to. The curve passed through that point without turning around. It rose, and it kept rising, straight through the place where she had written maximum in her own tidy capitals.

"That's not a maximum," she said.

"Now you know why I asked."

"But the derivative is zero there. I checked it twice." She rechecked it a third time, pencil moving fast, the wobbly table rocking under her knee. Zero. The arithmetic was clean. "The derivative is zero and the graph keeps going up through it. Both of those are true."

"Both are true," Dominic agreed. He was drinking his coffee with the composure of someone who had made this mistake himself, once, in a quieter room, and had never fully eulogized the version of himself who had trusted the shortcut. He would not tell her that. He only said, "So the method tells you where to look. It doesn't tell you what you found."

Maelie drew a small bracket around the point and wrote not a max beside it, then crossed out the word maximum at the top of the page, then felt stupid about the crossing out because the page was now a lugubrious gray mess of erased certainties, the genus of schoolwork she most despised, the kind that recorded her errors rather than her thinking. She copied the problem onto a fresh sheet instead.

"So the zero derivative is like the store bell," she said slowly. "It tells you the door opened. It doesn't tell you whether anyone walked in."

"That's better than my version."

"Then what's the actual maximum? There has to be one, the question asks for one."

"Not every question that asks has an answer shaped like the asking."

She looked at him. Behind him, Ms. Papadopoulos was locking the till early, counting coins into paper rolls, and the fluorescent light hummed the way it always did in the last hour, as if the store itself were winding down. Maelie read the problem again from the top, the whole thing, the units, the constraints, the sentence at the end she had skipped the first time because she had decided it was decoration.

"There's a domain," she said. "X has to be between zero and six hundred." She plotted the endpoints. The function rose all the way to the end of its allowed world and stopped. The maximum was sitting at the boundary, plain as a doorstop, at six hundred units, where the derivative was not zero at all.

"So the maximum is where the graph stops, not where it flattens," she said. "Depending on the function."

"Depending," Dominic said. He finished his coffee and crushed the cup. "That part you'll have to keep deciding."

Maelie wrote it at the bottom of the fresh page, and Ms. Papadopoulos called out from the register, "Eleven o'clock, you two," and turned the sign.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Mise en place is a French cooking term meaning 'putting in place': measuring and preparing all the ingredients before starting to cook.
story:
The recipe card sat propped against the flour tin, its florid cursive looping off the edges the way Gran's handwriting always did, as though the words themselves had wanted more room than the paper allowed. Kate had chosen the lemon cake because it was the one card with a coffee ring on it, a fossil of some supper twenty years ago, and because she wanted, before she left for college in the fall, to make something of Gran's with her own hands. Gran was asleep in the back room with the radio murmuring, and the house had that particular hush of a Tuesday afternoon, the clock in the hall counting out seconds like it had all the time in the world.

She creamed the butter and sugar first because that was the part she remembered from other kitchens, other winters. The mixer was older than she was and rattled like it might portend an early death, but it held. Zest, then juice, the lemon giving up its smell so suddenly that the whole kitchen seemed to shift seasons. She was halfway to folding in the dry ingredients, spoon lifted, before she read the next line and stopped.

There were no eggs on the counter. She checked the fridge, whose door still stuck the way it had when she was seven, then the pantry with its towers of tins, then the cold shelf in the cellar where Gran kept things that didn't seem to exist anywhere else. Three eggs, the card said. She had zero, and the batter sat behind her going flat.

She called Hazel from the hallway, keeping her voice down out of respect for the nap. "Do you know if you can skip eggs in a cake or does it just become a pancake with ambitions?"

"You've already mixed it?" Hazel's laugh crackled down the line. "You didn't check first?"

"There were lemons. I got excited." Kate looked back at the batter bowl, at her own hands dusted with flour, and felt the specific stupidity of a person who has done this before and somehow expected a different result. Hazel's family was away at her brother's tournament, forty minutes in the wrong direction, so Kate thanked her, hung up, and stood in the kitchen wondering whether a cake could ever be an affidavit of care if it arrived as a sad citrus puddle.

The neighbour, Ms. Qureshi, was watering pots of basil along the fence that separated the two gardens, and she waved when Kate leaned over the gate. Kate explained the situation in a rush, the missing eggs, the sleeping grandmother, the half-mixed batter, and Ms. Qureshi laughed in a way that suggested she had lived through several versions of this exact afternoon.

"My mother would have skinned me," she said, and went inside, returning with three eggs cupped in one hand like a small offering. "You know there's a name for what you didn't do. Mise en place. French. It means putting in place, measuring and preparing all the ingredients before you start to cook." She said it lightly, the way you'd hand over a tool, not a lecture. "Everything out, everything measured, then you begin."

Kate carried the eggs back across the garden holding them with a care she usually reserved for her phone, and while she beat them into the batter she turned the phrase over. Mise en place. She had always thought of cooking as her kind of thing precisely because it forgave improvisation, because you could throw yourself at it and fix things on the way down. Gran cooked the opposite way, everything cut before the pan was hot, the counter arranged like a small orderly city. Kate had privately filed that under old-person caution. Now she stood in the middle of the evidence, three borrowed eggs in a batter that had waited unprotected for twenty minutes, and wondered whether the two ways of thinking were really opposites or just different guesses about the same question. Maybe the preparation wasn't caution at all. Maybe it was what made the improvising possible, the way a bannister isn't there to stop you walking but to make the stairs something you don't have to think about.

The oven ticked as it heated. Kate spooned the batter into the tin Gran always used, the dented one with the pale ring inside it, and slid it in. While the cake rose she did something she had never done before: she took out the card for the shortbread, the one for the soup, the one for the apple tart, and she read each one all the way to the end, ingredient by ingredient, before she so much as touched a bowl. It felt strangely like reading ahead in a book you'd already started, like admitting that knowing the ending didn't spoil anything but steadied you for the middle.

Gran woke to the smell and came into the kitchen in her cardigan, hair pressed flat on one side, and stood at the oven door for a long moment saying nothing. "You used the good tin," she said finally, which in Gran's language was a paragraph.

"There's shortbread next," Kate said. "I checked. We're out of everything I'd need to get wrong." She set the butter out to soften and lined up the sugar, the flour, the fork for the holes in the top, each thing in its place on the counter, and then she took down the card and read it through one more time anyway, just to see what she'd missed.

activity: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
knowledge_domain: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
fact: Air resistance slows real projectiles, so a thrown ball usually lands shorter than the calculation that ignores air resistance predicts.
story:
The dining table still smelled of the lemon polish his mother used on Saturdays, and Jonathan had covered half of it with graph paper by nine in the evening. He was building a ball launcher out of a mousetrap, two dowels, and a spoon from the drawer, because Ms. Balogun had announced the projectile contest three days earlier and he had decided, without telling anyone, that he would win it. The plan was simple: solve the equations, set the launch angle, hit the target at the far end of the gymnasium floor.

He had spent the whole weekend learning to split a velocity into pieces. Horizontal and vertical, independent of each other, the way a thrown ball rises and falls along one axis while drifting steadily along the other. On Monday evening the equations had felt like a foreign alphabet. By Tuesday he could move through them, and by Wednesday the numbers came almost without effort, as if his brain had finally metabolized the method and could spend its attention elsewhere. He calculated a launch angle of forty-two degrees and a range of six point one meters, and he wrote both numbers on the masking tape along the gym floor with a fat marker.

Alec came over Thursday night with two energy drinks and no homework. "You're actually going to aim it with math," he said, turning the launcher over in his hands.

"That's the entire point."

"Diya's just going to eyeball hers."

"Diya's going to be short." Jonathan took the launcher back, set the trap arm, and laid a marble in the spoon.

They tested it in the hallway. He measured from the front door to the landing spot with a tape measure, three times, and each time the marble stopped at five meters and change, well short of what the paper promised. He knelt there with the tape stretched between his hands, and the incipient doubt he had been holding off all week finally had somewhere to stand.

He remembered then, without wanting to, a Saturday two summers ago when his uncle had taken him to the driving range. His uncle had watched him slice ball after ball into the net and said only, "The ball never goes as far as you think it should, does it," and Jonathan had nodded as if he understood, though he hadn't, and the bucket had run out before either of them said anything else.

He did not think of that afternoon as an explanation. He thought of it as something that had been waiting.

In the gym on Friday, Diya's launcher sent her ball tumbling end over end and it landed short too, and she laughed and adjusted by feel, moving her whole apparatus forward half a meter. Jonathan stood at his tape mark with his equations and his two true numbers, six point one on paper, five meters and change in the hallway, and he understood that both were honest. The equations were not wrong. They described a cleaner world than the one containing his marble, his spoon, and the air of the hallway.

Ms. Balogun walked the line of launchers with her clipboard. When she reached him she looked at his graph paper, then at his tape mark. "Your prediction and your result don't match," she said. It wasn't a question.

"The calculation ignores air resistance," Jonathan said. "Air resistance slows real projectiles, so a thrown ball usually lands shorter than the calculation predicts." He heard the words come out steadier than he felt. "I measured the difference in my hallway. I moved the launcher up by the gap."

She wrote something, and her face gave nothing away.

Diya's turn was last. Her ball arced high, drifted, and knocked the target can off its stand, and the side of the gym went up with Alec's whistle and the sound of the can rolling a long way across the varnished floor. She turned around with her arms up, looking for someone to be smug at, and found Jonathan.

He had moved his launcher forward by the measured gap. He had aimed at the can. His release was clean, the ball rose along the line he had drawn in his head a hundred times, and it came down a hand's width from the metal, close enough that the ball's landing sent a small shudder through the can without toppling it. Alec exhaled. Somewhere behind them Ms. Balogun made another mark on her clipboard, and Jonathan could not read her pen from where he stood, could not tell whether the mark was for the can he hadn't hit or the six-tenths of a meter he could account for.

Afterward he carried the launcher out to the parking lot with the spoon still twitching a little in its released arm, and Diya caught up to him at the curb.

"So you knew the exact number it would be short by," she said.

"I knew what it was short by in my hallway. The gym's different."

"Meaning you're guessing again."

"Meaning I'm guessing with better information."

She looked at the launcher, then at him. "Rematch at my house. My hallway's longer."

activity: taking a first driving lesson
knowledge_domain: taking a first driving lesson
fact: In a car with anti-lock brakes, a driver in an emergency should press the brake firmly and hold it rather than pump it, and can still steer.
story:
Sadie's grandfather had insisted on riding along for her first lesson, wedged into the back seat of the family car with his hands folded on his knees, and he had not stopped talking since they left the driveway. He was a garrulous man at the best of times, and the occasion had emancipated him from even his usual restraint; he narrated every mailbox they passed as though it were a landmark of personal significance. Ms. Rajapakse, the instructor, sat in the passenger seat with her own set of pedals folded discreetly under her feet and said, "Turn left at the lights, Sadie, and while you do, tell me what you're checking."

"Mirror, signal, shoulder," Sadie said, and did all three, and the turn came out cleaner than she had expected, the wheel returning to center under her palms like something that wanted to be there. She had read the whole owner's manual the night before, cover to cover, partly because she could not sleep and partly because she liked knowing things before anyone asked her to know them. One page had stayed with her, a paragraph about the anti-lock brakes, and she had read it twice.

"Grace, tell her about the brakes," her grandfather said from the back, leaning forward between the seats. "If you ever have to stop quick, you pump them. Tap, tap, tap. That's how we did it. Otherwise you lock up and you go wherever the car wants to go."

"That was true once," Ms. Rajapakse said, but she didn't continue, because she believed learners should find things out, and she looked at Sadie instead with an expression that Sadie had already learned to read as a question.

"The manual says the opposite," Sadie said slowly, working it through as she spoke. "With anti-lock brakes, in an emergency you press the brake firmly and hold it, and you can still steer while it's doing whatever it does. Pumping is the old way." Her grandfather started to object and then stopped himself, hand raised in the air like a man hailing a taxi that had already passed. "Dad's Corolla didn't have them," he admitted at last. "Neither did the truck. Huh."

They drove on through the Sunday-quiet streets behind the plaza, past the shuttered garden center and the church with the gravel lot, and Sadie felt the two versions of the truth sitting side by side in the car, her grandfather's hands and the manual's page, neither one dishonest, both of them earned in different decades. She could not tell yet which she would trust with her own foot, and she said so, and Ms. Rajapakse said, "Good. Keep the question open. Now, three-point turn at the cul-de-sac."

It was on the way back, on Marigold Street where the oaks narrowed the light into coins on the asphalt, that the boy's ball rolled out between two parked cars and the boy himself came after it, low and fast and sudden as a thrown thing. Sadie's whole body wanted to do six things at once. She pressed the brake hard and kept it pressed, felt the pedal shudder under her foot like something alive and refusing to be gentle, and she steered, because the manual said she could, easing the wheel so the car swung its nose away from the curb. The car stopped. The boy stopped, one sneaker on the asphalt, and looked at them with enormous offended eyes before grabbing his ball and retreating between the cars.

Nobody spoke for the length of the block. Then her grandfather leaned forward and put his hand briefly on Sadie's shoulder, and Ms. Rajapakse said, "You held it. You steered. That's exactly it." Sadie's hands were shaking on the wheel, small tremors like water settling, and she did not feel proud so much as rearranged, a person whose foot now knew something her mind had only memorized. She was still not sure she would be that calm a second time, and she was honest with herself about the uncertainty, letting it ride along with her the way her grandfather was riding in the back.

"Pull in at the next curb," Ms. Rajapakse said. "You've earned the parking practice." Her grandfather settled back, and after a moment he offered, almost shyly, that his father used to say an epigram about driving, something about the road forgiving nothing, and he couldn't quite remember how it went. "Probably just as well," he said. Sadie eased toward the curb, checked her mirror, and began the slow business of fitting the car between the painted lines.

activity: to weigh two historians' differing explanations of the Cold War against the evidence
knowledge_domain: to weigh two historians' differing explanations of the Cold War against the evidence
fact: In We Now Know, published in 1997 after Soviet archives had partly opened, Gaddis placed much more responsibility on Stalin personally for the Cold War.
story:
The essay was due Monday, and Justine had brought her books to her grandfather's house because his kitchen table was bigger than any surface at home and because nobody there would interrupt her except to refill her tea. She spread the two paperbacks side by side. The first, from the library, was Gaddis's older account of the Cold War's origins. The second, We Now Know, she had bought used, its spine cracked at the chapter on Stalin. Ms. Cruz had assigned the comparison in late September, standing at the whiteboard with her arms crossed, and had said only, "Notice what changes and what doesn't."

What Justine noticed, forty minutes into the afternoon, was that the same historian had changed his mind. The older book spread responsibility across the great powers, structures and systems pushing against each other. In We Now Know, published in 1997 after Soviet archives had partly opened, Gaddis placed much more responsibility on Stalin personally for the Cold War. She read the sentence twice, then a third time, then checked the publication dates again as though the years might rearrange themselves. Somewhere in the living room her grandfather had the television on low, and the somnolence of the commentary drifted toward her like something she could drown in.

She texted Ashton, who had the same assignment and a habit of answering in fragments. "did u get to the part where he basically takes it all back?" Ashton replied, "not took back. revised. big difference." Then, a minute later: "my dad says changing your mind is for losers." Justine put the phone face down and looked at her notes, which were now a map of arrows and question marks, and felt the problem take its actual shape: not what caused the Cold War, but how to weigh an explanation offered before the evidence against one offered after it, by the same man, with the same fluency.

Her grandfather came in to rinse his mug. He was eighty-one and moved like the kitchen was familiar country he crossed slowly on purpose. "You look belligerent," he said, nodding at her posture, at the pen she was gripping like a weapon.

"I'm not fighting a person," she said. "I'm fighting two books by the same person. One of them says the Cold War came out of the situation, and the newer one says it was Stalin, mostly, and I have to say which one the evidence supports, except the evidence is also just... one man's reading of it."

Her grandfather dried the mug and set it on the counter with the care of someone who had outlived several arguments. "When I changed my mind about things," he said, "it was never because someone won. It was because something happened that I couldn't look away from." He didn't say what, and she didn't ask, and he went back to the living room, and she understood he had given her a direction rather than an answer, which was his way.

She tried writing the paragraph she thought Ms. Cruz wanted, the confident one, where the archives settled it. She got three sentences in and stopped, because the sentence in front of her claimed more than the sentence in the book did. Gaddis had argued; he had not litigated the question to a finish, and neither, she realized, could she. She crossed it out and started over, this time laying the two explanations side by side the way the books lay on the table, letting the reader see the hinge between them: the same historian, before the Soviet archives had partly opened and after, moving weight from circumstance onto one man. What she owed Ms. Cruz was not a verdict but an account of why the weight moved, and where it still wobbled.

By the time the light went amber across the table, she had a page and a half. She had argued that the second explanation was stronger not because it was newer but because it answered more of what the first one left awkwardly unexplained, and she had admitted, in a final paragraph she almost deleted, that she couldn't fully separate the force of the argument from the force of new evidence appearing to confirm a person's capacity for ruin, which felt, uncomfortably, like a way of wanting history to have a face. Ashton texted again: "essay done. blamed stalin. easy." Justine looked at her own ending, its honest unfinished edge, and decided she would keep it. She closed the notebook, carried it to the doorway, and stood a moment watching her grandfather asleep in his chair with the television murmuring. "Grandpa," she said, "I think I finished." One of his eyes opened. "Then make the tea," he said.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: A Hanukkah menorah has nine branches: eight for the nights of the holiday and one for the shamash, the helper candle used to light the others, one more each night.
story:
Sarah had told Erin she couldn't come to the street festival tonight because of family obligations, which was true in the way that a half-truth is true: there was family, and there were obligations, and the two happened to be the same thing. Her mother wanted them at the community menorah lighting on Delancey Street by six, and Sarah wanted to want that, and for most of the walk over she almost did. The street smelled like fried dough and fermenting cider from the autumn stalls the city had left standing after the harvest market, and the vendors had strung lights between the lampposts so that the whole block glowed like something rehearsed.

Her father carried the box with their own menorah in it, the florid brass one with the curling stems that had been her grandmother's, because the rabbis had asked families to bring theirs for the long table near the stage. Sarah's little brother ran ahead toward the funnel cake stand. Her mother walked with that particular slowness she used when she wanted Sarah to slow down too, and Sarah matched it out of politeness and resentment, both, without sorting them apart.

The community menorah stood nine feet tall on the stage, and Sarah noticed, counting almost against her own will, that it had nine branches. Eight in a row and one lifted higher at the side. She was still counting when Richard appeared out of the crowd with a paper cup of cider and the grin he used when he'd been looking for her specifically.

"Erin said you had obligations," he said.

"I do. I'm at them."

"So this is them." He looked at the stage, at the families laying coats over folding chairs, at her brother negotiating with their father for cake. "I was at the other end of the street and saw the lights and it was, I don't know, synchronicity, because I was literally just reading about this in world history."

Sarah had prepared several versions of this conversation on the walk over and none of them started this way. "Reading about what?"

"Hanukkah. We have a quiz Monday." He said it lightly, the way he said most things, so she couldn't tell whether he was mocking the quiz or himself for studying, or neither.

The rabbi was calling families forward because the fourth night was about to begin, and Sarah's father was already waving her toward the table where their menorah sat among thirty others, hers the most ornamented and, she thought, the least honest, all that decoration over a plain little duty. She left Richard with a promise to find him after and went, and her mother handed her the box of candles, and this was the part Sarah actually loved, though she'd never said so to anyone at school: the narrow beeswax candles, the smell of them, the match her father always let her strike.

And then, kneeling at the table with the candles in her hand, she lost count. She had set in the shamash and three others and was reaching for a fourth when a boy at the next menorah knocked his table and candles rolled everywhere, and when she looked back at her own holders she couldn't remember whether the last candle she'd placed had been the third or the fourth. She counted what stood there. Four. But had one of them been the helper, the tall one, or was that still lying in the box?

Her father was talking to someone. The rabbi was already saying the blessing two tables down, which meant the room's attention was sliding toward the lighting, which meant she had under a minute.

"Every menorah has nine branches," Richard said, arrived at her elbow without her hearing him. "Eight for the eight nights, plus the shamash, the helper candle, the one you light the others with. So you put in one more each night, plus the helper. We literally just learned it."

She looked at her menorah. The shamash's holder was the raised one at the side, and it was empty. So the four she'd placed were all in a row, and tonight was the fourth night, and she needed one more plus the helper. Five candles burning tonight, total. She set the fifth, then the shamash, and her hands were steady, and when her father turned back she was already holding the match.

Afterward, walking the edge of the festival with the candle smoke still on her fingers, she found she couldn't decide what she felt about any of it, whether the excuse to Erin had been a lie or a kindness, whether wanting Richard there made the evening more hers or less. Her brother came running up with powdered sugar on his chin and grabbed her hand and pulled her toward the stage where the paper lanterns were being lit one by one down the whole length of the street.

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: Mexico's Day of the Dead is traditionally celebrated on November 1 and 2, when families build ofrendas, or home altars, with photos and the favorite foods and drinks of relatives who have died.
story:
The hospital had told them eleven o'clock, and Samuel's mother had repeated it twice, as though the number were fragile. He sat in the corridor outside the room where his grandmother lay, not going in, telling himself he was waiting for the right moment, though the truth was that he had been waiting for the right moment for two days and the moments kept sliding past him like trains he hadn't bought tickets for. Down the hall, a janitor's cart sat quiescent against the wall, one wheel turned slightly, as if it had been parked mid-thought.

Calista found him there. She had come with her mother, who was helping Samuel's mother with the paperwork, and she dropped into the chair beside him without asking if he wanted company. "You haven't gone in," she said.

"I went in this morning." He had. For almost a minute. He had stood at the door and counted the tiles on the floor, nineteen of them between him and the bed, and then a nurse had needed the room and he had stepped aside, and afterward he described it to himself as having visited.

Calista looked at him the way she looked at proofs she didn't believe. "My mom says your grandmother lived with you since you were six."

"So?"

"So you've been saying goodbye for ten years. One more afternoon isn't going to kill you." She pulled her phone out, then put it back. "Actually. My abuela would say you're doing it wrong anyway."

Samuel turned. "Doing what wrong?"

"Goodbyes. Mexicans don't really do them the way you're doing them, sitting in a hallway." She traced a circle on her knee with her finger. "Day of the Dead is November first and second. My family builds an ofrenda, a home altar, and we put out photos and the favorite foods and drinks of relatives who died. My tío gets his tequila. Every year, same bottle, same glass."

"That's not goodbye, then," Samuel said. "That's hello."

She shrugged. "Maybe that's the point."

He went in that afternoon because of Maximilian, who arrived at the hospital straight from practice, still in his cleats, carrying two paper cups of the terrible vending machine hot chocolate. Maximilian set one on the windowsill near the bed without ceremony, and that was what undid Samuel more than anything had: someone treating the room like a kitchen. "My mom texted yours," Maximilian said, as if that explained the hot chocolate. "She said your grandmother liked this stuff. From the machine at her work. She used to buy two."

"She never told me that," Samuel said.

"She told my mom. People tell the mothers of other kids the things they don't tell their own."

Later, at home, his mother stood in the kitchen not knowing what to do with her hands. The hospital had given them until Friday to clear out the things in the room, and the house felt expropriated, emptied of a government it had run under for a decade. Samuel said, "I want to build one of those altars. Calista told me about them. November first and second. An ofrenda. We'd put out her photo and her favorite food and drink."

His mother said, "We're not Mexican."

"We're not anything," Samuel said. "We don't do anything. She didn't do anything, that was her whole thing, she thought rituals were for people who couldn't handle real life, and now she's dead and we're just going to handle it."

His mother looked at him for a long time. "Get the pan dulce from the bread box," she said finally. "The concha. It's from Tuesday. It was hers. She was saving it."

He brought the sweet bread out and set it on the table between them, the sugar topping cracked down the middle like a fault line. She had been saving it, which meant she had been looking forward to it, which meant there had been a future she'd assumed. He arranged the bread on a plate and went upstairs for the photograph from her bedside, the one from before he was born, and when he came back down his mother had lit a candle she'd found somewhere, and Maximilian's hot chocolate cup was still in his jacket pocket, and he took it out and placed it next to the bread.

"That's from the hospital," his mother said.

"I know what it's from."

She didn't move it. November was three weeks away and the bread would be gone by then, and he understood that they'd have to buy more, that the whole thing was a kind of pretending, and that pretending might be its own meritocracy, where the effort counted for the belief. Or it might be nothing. He couldn't tell yet and he was tired of deciding.

Calista texted him a photo of her family's altar, candles and marigolds and a glass of tequila for a man he'd never met. He set his phone beside the plate, screen up.

"So what do we do on the first?" his mother asked.

"You eat the bread," he said. "I think you just eat the bread."

activity: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
knowledge_domain: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
fact: Table salt, sodium chloride, has a molar mass of about 58.44 grams per mole.
story:
Loic stood behind his folding table in the gymnasium with a five-kilogram bag of table salt, a kitchen scale, and a poster that read, in letters he had painted at eleven the night before, HOW MUCH SALT IS REALLY IN THERE? He had not slept well and the gym smelled like floor wax and someone else's vinegar volcano.

"Interesting," said Ms. Chen, pausing at his table with a clipboard. She taught chemistry two floors above him and had agreed to judge even though, she said, the physics display with the Tesla coil made her nervous. "How much is really in there in what sense?"

"In moles," Loic said. "Like, everyone says grams, but grams are just weight. I wanted to know the actual number of particles. Sort of."

Ms. Chen wrote something on her clipboard that he could not read upside down, which was the point of clipboards, and moved on to the exhibit about bridge design.

The problem had started three weeks earlier in his kitchen. His father, who read popular science books and repeated their claims at dinner, had announced that sodium chloride had a molar mass of about 58.44 grams per mole, and that if Loic ever learned anything useful in school it should be how to use that number. Loic had said fine, and then realized he did not know how, and had been annoyed about it ever since, because his father was right often enough to be irritating.

Bruno arrived at the table holding a funnel cake he had bought from the booster club table near the doors. "You're the salt guy," he said. "Claudia told me. She said you had a crisis about it."

"I didn't have a crisis. I had an unsolved problem." Loic tapped the scale. "Here, weigh something. I need to demonstrate."

Bruno set down the funnel cake, wiped his hands on his jeans, and weighed out a small pile of salt, which came to 58.5 grams, give or take the crumbs already on the paper. "Okay," Bruno said. "So what?"

"So look at the poster."

The poster had two columns. One said GRAMS, which everyone understood, and one said MOLES, which was the one Loic had spent the weekend on. At the top he had written the conversion as he had worked it out himself, on paper, after his father's comment and after a very unhelpful argument with Bruno about whether a "mole" was an animal, a spy, or a unit. It was a unit. You divided the mass by the molar mass, and the grams cancelled, and what was left was moles. He had checked it against his textbook at two in the morning, feeling something between triumph and the suspicion that he had only codified what everyone else already knew.

"That pile," Loic said, pointing at Bruno's 58.5 grams, "is almost exactly one mole. A mole of salt is 58.44 grams."

"How many of those in the bag?" Claudia had come up behind them with her own poster rolled under her arm; her project was on the epidemiology of a flu outbreak at their middle school, and she was sanguine about her chances in a way Loic found either reassuring or grating depending on the hour.

"I did the math. The bag's five kilos. Five thousand grams divided by 58.44." He turned the poster around to show the long division he had done in pencil and then gone over in marker so it would read from a distance. "About eighty-five and a half moles. Eighty-five point five, roughly. I rounded."

"You rounded," Claudia repeated. "Bold."

"It's a five-kilo bag from the supermarket. It's not a laboratory."

The gym got louder as more visitors came through. A man in a coach's jacket stopped, looked at the poster for a long moment, and said, "My wife puts that stuff on everything," and left before Loic could respond, which Loic decided to count as engagement.

Ms. Chen came back around near the end, when the Tesla coil had gone off twice and the bridge people were arguing with the volcano people about noise. "So," she said. "Why does it matter, the moles? Why not just say you have five kilograms?"

Loic looked at the pile Bruno had weighed, still sitting on the paper, starting to clump slightly in the humid air. He had a prepared answer about particles and about how grams told you how heavy something was but moles told you how much of it there was, in the sense that mattered if you wanted anything to react with anything. He had rehearsed it in the car. Instead he said, "Because grams are just what the scale says. The moles are the actual amount. The scale doesn't know what it's weighing."

Ms. Chen wrote on her clipboard, and this time she tilted it so he could see.
