The note said he should come by the chemistry room on Monday, and that she had a borrowed balance that measured to four decimal places, and that his estimate of eighty-five point five moles was close but the bag itself weighed a little more than the salt in it.

"The bag?" Loic said.

"The bag," Ms. Chen said, and moved on toward the Tesla coil with the expression of someone who had judged science fairs for a long time and no longer surprised herself.

Bruno picked up his funnel cake, which had gone cold. Claudia unrolled her poster and propped it against the edge of his table without asking. Loic stood there with the salt, the scale, and the sudden problem of the bag's own weight, and began, in the margin of the poster, a new column of numbers.

activity: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
knowledge_domain: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
fact: Between large parallel plates the field is nearly uniform, so away from the edges a point near one plate has the same field strength as a point midway between them.
story:
The physics lab smelled of warm dust and the lemon cleaner the janitor used on Fridays, and Sebastian had commandeer of the equipment trolley, which meant Filip kept trying to steal the metre stick back while Jakob copied the diagram from the board. Two brass plates stood upright on the bench, clamped an insulating distance apart, wired to a supply Mr. Bekele had set humming before he retreated to his desk and his marking.

"The task," Mr. Bekele had said, "is the field strength at a point between the plates. Take the point where I've marked it. The apparatus is yours. Do not burn anything." He had drawn an X on a slip of paper taped to a third clamp, positioned closer to one plate than the other, and Sebastian had understood immediately what the X was for: he needed the distance from the point to each plate, because surely the field near a plate must be stronger there, the way the ground is steeper near the bottom of a hill.

So he measured. From the X to the left plate, then to the right, Filip holding the metre stick steady while Sebastian read off millimetres twice because the first reading felt wrong. Jakob wrote both numbers in his rounded handwriting and drew a little box around them, and for twenty minutes they argued about which distance went into the numerator and which into the denominator, Sebastian insisting on the nearer plate, Filip on the farther, each of them half-guessing.

Sebastian's father had been put on furlough in March, and the house had gone quiet in a way that had nothing to do with sound; the television stayed off, the chairs were pushed in more carefully. His father sat some evenings at the kitchen table with the laptop open to job listings, and once, when Sebastian asked about his homework, his dad had said, without looking up, "Do it properly. You can't control the rest." It wasn't advice so much as a fact stated at the table, and Sebastian had carried it to school like a stone in a pocket whose weight he kept checking.

In the lab, Mr. Bekele drifted past their bench and looked at the two circled distances, and looked at the X, and said nothing. He picked up the spare probe, set it down again a little nearer the middle of the gap, and walked away. Sebastian stared at that probe. He moved the X's clamp, sliding the point closer to the midpoint between the plates, and read the meter, and read it again, and then moved the point back near the left plate and read it once more.

"It's the same," he said. "Jakob. It's the same number."

Jakob came over, skeptical, arms folded like someone owed money. Sebastian moved the point again, midway, near the left plate, midway. The needle barely shivered. "Between plates like these," Sebastian said slowly, working it out as he spoke, "the field is uniform. Away from the edges. A point near one plate has the same field strength as a point midway between them." The words felt strange in his mouth, like reciting something in a language he had only just begun to think in.

"It can't be," Filip said, and measured the distances himself, all four of them, as though the metre stick owed him an explanation. It didn't. The distances were different and the readings were not, and the two numbers in Jakob's careful boxes were, in the end, worth nothing, which was somehow both galling and freeing. They had spent half the lesson on a quantity that never entered the answer. Sebastian looked through the window at the arboreal line of poplars along the fence, their leaves moving all together in the wind, uniformly, and thought that the field was like that, the same everywhere it mattered, indifferent to where you stood inside it.

He copied the single result into his book. The gain sat next to the cost in his head: the answer was right and the afternoon was gone, and he still couldn't have said why the field behaved that way, only that it did, the way his father sat at the table. Mr. Bekele collected their sheets, paused at Sebastian's, and drew a small check mark beside the lone number. Filip snapped the metre stick shut. "So next time," he said, "we just don't measure anything?"

activity: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
knowledge_domain: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
fact: The Situation-Behavior-Impact model, from the Center for Creative Leadership, frames feedback by naming when it happened, what the person did, and what effect it had.
story:
Ashley found the worksheet in her jacket pocket at Seerat's birthday party, folded twice and soft at the creases from a week of being carried around. It had come from a leadership workshop Mr. Wanjiru ran on Thursdays after practice, the one half the team attended only because he brought samosas. She had shoved it in her pocket intending to read it and then kept not reading it, the way she kept not saying the thing she needed to say to Terrance.

The party had spilled from Seerat's kitchen onto the porch, where someone's playlist competed with the neighbor's sprinkler. Ashley stood near the screen door holding a cup of punch she wasn't drinking, watching Terrance attempt to teach a freshman the chest pass against the garage door. He was good at that, the teaching. He was generous with everyone except when it came to the actual games.

For two weeks now she had been carrying a sentence she hadn't delivered. In the third quarter against Riverside, with forty seconds left and the score tied, Terrance had waved off her cut and forced a pass into a seam that wasn't there. The turnover had cost them the game. She'd rehearsed versions in her head. "You're a ball hog" was one. "You never trust me" was another. Each one felt true and each one, she suspected, would only make him flinch and shut down, and she needed him open, because there was a rematch in ten days and she intended to win it.

Seerat found her on the porch steps and sat down, heels hooked on the middle rung. "You're doing the face," Seerat said. "The one where you're writing an essay nobody asked for."

"I'm trying to figure out how to say something to Terrance without it turning into a fight."

"About the Riverside game." Seerat said it flatly, not as a question, and Ashley realized the whole team had been circling the same unsaid thing. Seerat nodded at the paper sticking out of her pocket. "What's that?"

Ashley unfolded it. The workshop had gone through the Center for Creative Leadership's Situation-Behavior-Impact model, which framed feedback by naming when it happened, what the person did, and what effect it had. Mr. Wanjiru had made them rewrite sentences on the board, and Ashley remembered Deshawn turning "you're lazy" into a comment about one missed deadline, and how strange it was that the second version was harder to argue with and easier to hear. The model had a laconic tidiness to it, three steps, no adjectives about anyone's character, and she had distrusted that tidiness at first. It felt like a way to sand the edges off honesty.

"That's actually why I took the samosas," Seerat said, reading over her arm. "My mom does debriefs at the hospital and she uses something like it. Except hers involves a lot more yelling, so." She laughed. "Go do it before you lose your nerve."

"What if I get it wrong and he just hears it as an attack anyway?"

"Then you'll know something you don't know now." Seerat stood, brushed crumbs off her jeans. "But you won't know standing here."

Terrance had given up on the freshman and was leaning against the garage, cup in hand. Ashley crossed the yard, and the smell of cut grass and chlorine from the sprinkler was suddenly very specific, the way things get when you're about to say something. He saw her coming and his face did a small wary thing, the tightening of someone who has been expecting a conversation and hoping it would never arrive. She knew he'd been expecting it. That was half of why she hadn't started it.

"Hey," she said. "You got a second?"

"Sure." He set the cup on the porch rail.

"In the fourth quarter against Riverside, with about forty seconds left." She made herself keep going. "You waved off my cut and passed into the middle, and it got picked off, and we lost the game." She stopped there. The model ended at impact and she understood now why: the moment you added "and you always" or "and you think," you stopped describing and started prosecuting.

Terrance was quiet for a second. His shoulders came down a fraction. "I thought Dobbins had slipped," he said. "I read it wrong. I didn't see you open." He looked at her, actually looked, the first time in two weeks. "You were open."

"I was wide open."

"I know." He rubbed the back of his neck. "You should've said something at the game."

"You're right, I should have." She heard herself say it and it was true, and it cost less than she'd expected. "The rematch's in ten days. I want us running the two-man game on that side. I think it works if we're both looking for it."

He was already nodding. "Run it in warmups tomorrow, see how it reads."

From the porch, Seerat raised her cup toward them, and Terrance raised his back, and Ashley went inside for more punch, the folded worksheet still in her pocket, no longer needed and somehow not thrown away either.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: Pierre de Coubertin designed the five Olympic rings in 1913, choosing colors so that every national flag of the time contained at least one of them, including the white background.
story:
Ms. Dela Cruz's television was the largest Chloe had ever sat in front of, and she wanted to be clear with herself, before anything else, that she had not wanted to come. She had said yes only because her mother had used that particular voice, the one that made refusal feel like a small crime, and because Noam had texted three times, and because the game was, after all, only a game. She did not care who won. She had told Donald as much on the walk over, twice, and if she had told him a third time it was only because the sidewalk was icy and talking kept her warm.

The living room was crowded in the way of a house that had decided, decades ago, exactly how many people it would hold and was now being argued with. Ms. Dela Cruz had dragged two folding chairs up from the basement and stationed them at the edge of the rug like lifeboats. Donald took one and immediately began excoriating the referee for a call made thirty seconds into the match, a red card that Chloe, from the doorway, honestly could not evaluate. She was not invested. She simply had a good view of the replay.

"Sit, sit," Ms. Dela Cruz said, pressing a bowl of plantain chips into her hands. Above the screen, on the wall, hung a small framed print of the Olympic rings, five interlocked circles in blue, yellow, black, green, and red, and Chloe found her eyes going up to it the way a tongue goes to a loose tooth. She had been staring at the rings all week, if she was being honest, which she was, mostly. The opening ceremony had swept past them on this same screen, and she had caught herself scanning the logo for the colors of her grandmother's flag, the blue and white she'd grown up seeing draped over a chair every fourth of July at the cousin's house. She had not found the white at first. That had bothered her more than she admitted to anyone, including, for a while, herself.

Noam arrived late, breathless, holding a bag of ice he had clearly dropped at some point, and wedged onto the arm of the couch beside Chloe. On the screen a midfielder went down in the box and the whole room rose at once, Ms. Dela Cruz's hands to her face, Donald shouting something in a language Chloe didn't know he spoke.

"Penalty," the commentator said, laconic, and the room collapsed back down like a wave retreating.

"Chloe," Noam said, not looking away from the screen, "you're doing the thing."

"I'm not doing anything."

"You're doing the flag thing. The rings thing." He reached across her for a chip. "You've been doing it since Tuesday."

She considered denying it, and then considered the fact that denial had stopped working somewhere around the second text. "Fine," she said. "The white bothers me. Our flag is basically white with stuff on it, and the rings are on that flag material anyway, but it feels like cheating. Like the white doesn't count."

Donald, who had apparently been listening while excoriating the opposing defender, turned around. "Wait, what?"

"The white background," Chloe said. "It counts. Look it up."

Donald looked it up. His phone lit the underside of his chin while the penalty was being set up, the kicker placing the ball with a terrible calm. "It says here the rings were designed in 1913 by Pierre de Coubertin," he read. "And he picked the colors so that every national flag at the time had at least one of them, including the white background."

"So the white does count," Chloe said.

"So the white does count," Donald agreed, and something in her chest loosened, which was ridiculous, because nothing had actually changed. Her flag was her flag whether or not a French baron had accounted for it over a hundred years ago. She knew that. And yet.

The kicker ran up and drove the ball low and hard, and the goalkeeper, diving the wrong way, got a hand to it, and the ball skimmed off his fingertips and in. The room detonated. Ms. Dela Cruz was on her feet, Donald had lifted the folding chair with him somehow, and Chloe found that she was standing too, both hands in the air, the bowl of chips tilting dangerously, shouting with the rest of them. She sat down quickly, as if the outburst had happened to someone else in her body.

"It's not about the rings," she said to Noam, quietly, under the roar.

"I didn't say it was."

"It's about wanting to be included in something and being told, actually, you always were. That's a reprieve, kind of. Like getting off the hook for a crime you didn't know you'd been accused of." She stopped. "That might be the wrong word."

"It might," Noam said. "But I get it."

What she could not get straight, even in her own head, was whether she believed the version of herself that didn't care or the version that was on her feet when the goal went in. Both were real; both had plantedain chips on Ms. Dela Cruz's rug. Maybe, she thought, watching the players reset at midfield, you could hold both, the way the rings held their separate colors and still made one figure, and maybe you never entirely settled which one you meant.

In the eighty-ninth minute a substitute, on for barely six minutes, rose alone at the far post and headed the equalizer past a stranded keeper, and Chloe was up again, no decision involved at all, spilling chips, grabbing Noam's sleeve.

"Tell me you saw that," she said.

activity: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
knowledge_domain: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
fact: In a standard repayment mortgage, early monthly payments go mostly toward interest, and later payments go mostly toward paying down the amount borrowed.
story:
The cheque was for two hundred and forty dollars, and Oliver had told his mother he would cash it at lunch, which was true, and that he would not speak to anyone at the bank about anything else, which was also true as far as it went. He had not said anything about the notice from the landlord, the one folded twice in his back pocket, the one about the rent going up in September. He was good at that distinction, between what he said and what he meant, and he told himself it wasn't lying so much as bookkeeping.

The branch on Marsh Street was spartan in a way that seemed deliberate, two tellers behind thick glass, a row of chairs bolted to the floor, a stand of pamphlets about savings accounts nobody had taken. Ruby was already there, waiting with her mother's deposit for the second time that week, because her mother worked doubles and trusted Ruby with the slip more than with the car. "Don't ask," Ruby said when Oliver joined her. "The line's moving and I have chem at one." He didn't ask. He watched her sign the back of her mother's cheque in the careful letters of a person impersonating her own mother, and thought that everyone in the building was probably impersonating somebody.

Two chairs down, Ms. Lombardi from their street sat with a mortgage statement spread across her knees, turning the pages back and forth as if one of them had to be wrong. Oliver knew her as the neighbour with the harsh opinion about other people's recycling bins. Now she looked smaller, reading glasses low on her nose, one finger moving down a column. She leaned toward the teller's window when it opened and her voice carried. "I've paid every month for five years. Five years. Look at the balance. I've barely made a dent in what I owe."

The teller said something quiet. Ruby glanced over and then at Oliver, and her eyebrows did the thing they did when she wanted to watch without looking like she was watching.

"How is that," Ms. Lombardi said, not quite a question, and the teller turned the statement sideways and pointed at two columns, one for interest, one for principal, and Oliver could not hear the rest but he could see the shape of it, the interest column fat and the principal column thin, month after month, and then further down the page, years down, the fat one thinning and the thin one fattening, like a river trading banks.

"That's the part nobody tells you," Ruby said when Ms. Lombardi had gathered her papers and gone. "My mom found out after three years. All those payments and the amount she owes just sits there, basically." She handed her deposit slip to the teller. "It's like the money goes in the front door and out the window."

Oliver cashed his cheque next, ninety of it into savings, the rest in twenties, and asked the teller what the rate was on a savings account, and she told him, and he asked whether there was a minimum for something like a down payment on a place, and she said the advisors upstairs could talk about that, and he said maybe later, which was a third kind of not-quite-lying. On the way out he took a pamphlet, because taking one was less noticeable than wanting one.

He read it on the bench outside while Ruby texted her mother. The pamphlet laid out the arithmetic of buying plainly, deposit, down payment, monthly payments stretched over decades, and it confirmed what the columns on Ms. Lombardi's statement had shown him: the first years of a mortgage mostly paid the interest, and only later did the payments swing toward what was actually owed. His mother had been saying for months that renting was throwing money away and buying was building something, and he had believed her because she said it with such certainty, and now the picture was less tidy. Renting paid for a roof he needed anyway. Buying paid the bank first, for a long time, before it paid him. He could hold both ideas at once and he could not make them agree, and he was honest enough with himself, on the bench, to admit which parts he was guessing at.

Ruby dropped onto the bench beside him and looked at the pamphlet upside down. "You're not buying anything," she said. "You're seventeen."

"I'm finding out how it works."

"For who?"

He thought of his mother's face at the kitchen table, the calculator, the folders of listings she'd printed at the library, and the notice in his back pocket, and he understood that he could not predicate any advice to her on what he'd learned here, not honestly, because he did not yet know whether the numbers were on her side or only her hope was. "For us," he said. "Maybe."

"Bring the notice to chem," Ruby said, standing, shouldering her bag. "We'll do the math at lunch, both columns. Mom likes that stuff." She was halfway to the corner before he remembered he'd never told her he had the notice with him.

He took it out and read it again under the streetlight, the September figure circled in the landlord's blue ink, and then he folded it the way he'd found it, put it in his pocket, and got up to catch the bus home.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: The 2026 FIFA World Cup, hosted by Canada, Mexico and the United States, was the first with 48 teams and the first hosted by three countries.
story:
The Kobayashis' living room smelled like burnt popcorn and cardamom, and by the time the national anthems started, every cushion had been claimed. Ms. Kobayashi had commandeered the good armchair for herself and her terrier, Biscuit, while Layla ended up on the floor between Kalan and Josephine with a bowl of chips balanced on her knee. On screen, the stadium glittered, and her father kept leaning forward to adjust the volume as though the match might improve if it were louder.

"This is the one," Kalan said, gesturing at the television with a handful of popcorn. "First World Cup with forty-eight teams. They expanded it."

Josephine made a skeptical noise from the couch. "Forty-eight? That's not an expansion, that's a fire hazard. Half those teams are going to get eliminated before they unpack their luggage." Her voice had that acerbic edge she reserved for Kalan specifically, which Layla found both funny and slightly exhausting, since it meant every neutral fact became a battlefield.

"It's not just teams, either," Layla said, mostly to keep the peace. "Three countries are hosting it. Canada, Mexico, the United States. Nobody's ever done that before." She'd read it on the tournament app two weeks ago and then, embarrassed by how much she cared, had closed the app and pretended she hadn't.

"Three hosts," Josephine repeated, as though Layla had confessed to a crime. "So who gets the final? Do they flip a coin? Rock, paper, scissors?" She launched into a bit about the three federations playing jan-ken-pon on the midfield line, and even Ms. Kobayashi laughed into her tea, which encouraged Josephine the way a spotlight encourages an actor.

Layla smiled, but something in her kept pulling in two directions. Part of her agreed with Josephine: forty-eight teams did dilute things, made the group stage feel like a long hallway before the actual rooms. She'd watched old matches with her mother, sixteen-team tournaments where every game arrived already soaked in consequence. But another part of her remembered the qualifying highlights she'd stumbled across at two in the morning, small nations celebrating draws like championships, players weeping on pitches she couldn't pronounce the names of. Forty-eight meant forty-eight chances to matter. She couldn't make those two feelings agree, and she wasn't sure she wanted to, because both seemed true.

"Kobayashi-style verdict," Ms. Kobayashi announced during halftime, standing with the solemnity of a judge. "The tournament is too big and also not big enough, and everyone at my party will now help eat the samosas before they get cold." She delivered this little oratory with such gravity that Biscuit barked, and Layla's father applauded, which started a chain reaction of applause that made the whole room ridiculous.

In the kitchen, fetching more ice, Layla found Josephine alone by the freezer. "You actually looked it up," Josephine said, not quite an apology. "Forty-eight, three countries. I just like arguing with Kalan."

"I know," Layla said. "I like arguing with you. That's the problem. I agreed with both of you all game." She said it lightly, but she meant it: she had spent the first half believing two opposite things, and instead of picking one, she'd somehow ended up holding both, like carrying two full cups through a crowd, waiting to see which one spilled first.

When they got back, the second half had already begun, and a team nobody at the party had heard of six months ago was stringing together passes like they'd invented the sport. Kalan was on his feet. Josephine was yelling something about fire hazards in a tone that had lost all its acid and become pure delight. Layla stood between them, chips abandoned, still undecided and completely happy about it. On the screen, the striker shaped to shoot, and the whole living room inhaled at once.

activity: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
knowledge_domain: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
fact: Electric field strength can be measured in volts per metre or in newtons per coulomb, and the two units are equivalent.
story:
The rumour going around was that Mr. Russo had failed his own physics degree, and Anna had repeated it often enough that she half believed she'd witnessed the failure herself. She had not. She had heard it in Year 10 from a girl whose name she'd forgotten, and it had coloured everything since, the way a jaundiced eye colours a whole room. Now Mr. Russo set the worksheets on the bench between her and Cadence and said only, "Between the plates. Show me the field at point P."

The lab smelled of warm dust and the faint vinegar of old batteries. Two parallel plates sat in their holders on every bench, and Anna's task, which she had read three times without absorbing, was to compute the electric field strength at a point in the gap. Cadence was already writing, her pen moving with the confidence of someone copying a recipe she had made before. Leonardo, across the aisle, kept glancing over, which he did when he wanted to argue but not enough to start it himself.

"I've got it," Cadence said, underlining a number. "Twelve hundred newtons per coulomb."

"Volts per metre," Leonardo said, leaning over anyway. "I got twelve hundred volts per metre. So one of us is wrong."

They looked at each other with the particular fixed politeness of people about to be impolite. Cadence said she'd used force divided by charge, because that was what field meant, the push on each unit of charge. Leonardo said he'd used the voltage across the plates divided by the separation, because that was the formula on the board, and the board didn't lie. Anna, who in Year 10 had told Cadence that Leonardo copied his answers, watched him now writing out his method from nothing, unashamed, and felt the old rumour shift under her like a chair leg on a sloped floor.

"Ask Mr. Russo," Cadence said, and Anna didn't move, because she had told the class last week, confidently, that field strength was measured in newtons per coulomb, full stop. She'd said it the way she said most things, as if certainty were the same as knowledge. If Leonardo was right, she had spread an error, and if both were somehow right, then she had been right and wrong at once, which was worse, because it meant she hadn't understood what she was saying.

She took both sheets. She set Cadence's beside Leonardo's and followed each line with her finger, the force on the test charge, the potential difference, the distance between the plates, and the same twelve hundred arriving at the end of two entirely different roads. She sat with that for a moment. It felt like a trick, the kind of coincidence that only happens in textbooks, and then it felt like something else: like discovering that two people describing the same house from opposite streets had been arguing about whether it had a front door or a back one.

"They're the same," she said. "Volts per metre and newtons per coulomb. They're equivalent. Same field, two names for it."

Leonardo looked at her as though she'd pronounced on something over her pay grade. Cadence looked at her as though she'd betrayed her, which, given the Year 10 remark about copying, was fair. "Then why didn't you say that last week," Cadence said, "when you told everyone it was newtons per coulomb?" It wasn't a question, and Anna didn't dress it up as one in her head. She had said it because saying things first had begun to matter more than saying them truly, and the perspicacity she'd been praised for since primary school had curdled into quickness, a talent for arriving early rather than for arriving right.

"You're right," Anna said. "I said more than I knew." She slid both worksheets back across the bench. "Twelve hundred either way. Both of you are right."

Mr. Russo drifted past their bench on his slow circuit, glanced at the two sheets without stopping, and tapped the gap between the plates once with his pen, the way a man might tap a door he expected to be locked. "Then argue about something worth arguing about," he said, and moved on. Cadence capped her pen. Leonardo, for once, said nothing. Anna copied both methods into her book, side by side, and left a narrow column of blank space between them, which she did not fill in.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: Many Orthodox churches, including the Russian Orthodox Church, celebrate Christmas on January 7 because they keep December 25 on the older Julian calendar.
story:
Hunter had told Gage he was busy on January 7, and Gage had asked, twice, busy with what, exactly, since Christmas had happened two weeks ago. "It happened for you," Hunter had said, pulling on his coat, and left it there, partly because it was fun to be mysterious and partly because he wasn't sure he could explain it without sounding like a textbook.

The community hall smelled of cabbage rolls and beeswax, which was the smell of his grandmother's entire side of the family, gathered now under paper stars taped to the ceiling. At the door a woman he didn't know pressed a honey-dipped cookie into his hand and said, "You have your grandfather's eyebrows," which was a strange way to begin an evening. He found his grandmother by the samovar, holding court.

"You're late," she said, though he was twenty minutes early.

"I'm exactly on time."

"By whose calendar?" she said, and cackled at her own joke, and he laughed too, because she laughed at it every year.

Here was the thing he'd had to work out for himself, since nobody in the family ever just told you anything. When he was nine, he'd asked why their Christmas came two weeks after the neighbors', and his grandmother had said, "We keep December 25, but on the old Julian calendar, so it falls on January 7," and he had nodded as if this settled everything, and then spent a week quietly convinced the whole thing was a family eccentricity, like the jar of buttons nobody was allowed to touch. Only later, at a cousin's baptism, had he heard the priest mention that many Orthodox churches, the Russian Orthodox among them, kept the same date on the same old calendar, and it had rearranged something in him. The late Christmas wasn't a quirk. It was a whole other room in the house of the world, and his family lived in it, and so, in a way, did he. He hadn't decided yet whether that was a thing he internalized or just a thing he knew, the way he knew the capital of a country he'd never visit.

"Stop standing there philosophizing," his grandmother said. "Take cookies to the boy by the window. He looks hungry and useless, like you."

The boy by the window was Gage.

"What," Hunter said. "How."

"Your mom told my mom," Gage said, taking three cookies. "You said it happened for me, and it didn't, so I came to see the version that happens for you. Also there's a girl here who beat me at chess in fourth grade and I want a rematch." He looked around at the icons propped on folding tables, the old men arguing about, as far as Hunter could tell, soup. "So this is your patrimony, huh."

"If you use words like that, my grandmother will adopt you."

"She already did. She called me a good boy with stupid hair, which from her is basically a hug."

Abdallah arrived an hour later with his little sister, because their parents were working and Ms. Sadeghi, who ran the tutoring center and apparently knew every family in a six-block radius, had said it was an open invitation. "I brought the leftover baklava from ours," Abdallah said, setting the tray beside the cabbage rolls like a diplomat presenting credentials, and the old men adopted the baklava instantly and unanimously.

It was during the singing that the twist came, though it took Hunter a moment to recognize it as one. The girl Gage wanted a rematch against turned out to be Gage's own cousin, whom he hadn't seen since fourth grade, and she beat him at chess twice more on a board someone produced from behind the stage curtains, and their argument about the second game grew so bellicose that the priest came over to watch, taking sides openly. But the actual twist was smaller. Hunter's grandmother settled into the chair beside him, tired from dancing, and said, "Your grandfather proposed to me at this feast. On January 7. I told him it was too early, we'd only known each other a year, and he said, 'By our calendar we're always a little behind, so we'd better start sooner.'" She patted his hand. "I said yes before the song ended."

Hunter looked at the paper stars, at Gage losing his rematch, at Abdallah's little sister teaching an old woman a clapping game. He still didn't know if the late Christmas was his, exactly, or something he was only holding for the family, the way you hold a coat. But he was here, and the cookies were warm, and next year, he thought, he'd ask Gage to come again without waiting for anyone's mother to arrange it.

"Same time, two weeks after everyone else," he said to Gage across the room, and raised his cup of tea.

"By whose calendar?" Gage shouted back, and the whole table laughed before either of them could.

activity: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
knowledge_domain: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
fact: Hans Krebs and William Johnson described the citric acid cycle in 1937, and Krebs shared the 1953 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for it.
story:
Jasmine had told everyone she didn't need the study group, and she had told them twice, which was already a kind of evidence against the claim. She brought her biology notebook to the community garden anyway, because the garden was where she went when she wanted to think, and because Ms. Das, who ran the compost bins on Saturdays, let her sit at the shaded table by the tool shed without asking questions. The midterm was Monday. Cellular respiration, glycolysis to the Krebs cycle to the electron transport chain, filled seven pages of her notes, most of them copied from Angelina, who had actually been awake in class.

Angelina and Royce arrived at eleven with a bag of clementines and no plan. "You said you had it handled," Angelina said, dropping onto the bench across from Jasmine.

"I do have it handled. I'm reviewing."

Royce peeled a clementine in one long spiral, which he could do and which he knew impressed people. "Then review out loud. Explain it to us. That's the thing Ms. Das is always saying, that teaching it is how you know you know it."

"That's metacognition," Jasmine said, pleased to have a word for it. "Thinking about your own thinking. I do that naturally." She did not mention that she had read the word on a poster in the guidance office two days ago and had been waiting to use it. "Fine. Glucose goes in. Six carbons. It gets split in half during glycolysis, and that happens in the cytoplasm, and it makes a little ATP and some NADH, and then the pyruvate moves into the mitochondria."

"The mitochondria," Angelina said. "Which are what, exactly?"

"The powerhouse of the cell." Jasmine said it flatly, because it was true and also the most tired sentence in biology. "They've got two membranes, an outer one and a folded inner one. The folds extrude inward, like fingers." She drew it in the dirt with a stick: a bean shape, then ridges inside the bean. Royce leaned over and added a smiley face to it, and she wiped that out with her palm.

"What happens inside, after glycolysis?" Angelina had her own notebook open now, and Jasmine could see that Angelina's diagram had arrows Jasmine's didn't.

"The Krebs cycle." Jasmine paused. She had a fact lodged somewhere in her head about the name, and she reached for it. "It used to be called something else. The tricarboxylic acid cycle. And Hans Krebs and William Johnson described the citric acid cycle in 1937." She said it with more certainty than she owned. "And Krebs won a Nobel Prize for it."

"Wait, actually?" Royce said.

"He shared the Nobel Prize. 1953. Physiology or Medicine." She was surer now, the way she got surer with each repetition, which was not the same as being correct, though she had no way of noticing that from inside.

"Why does a body process have a guy's name on it?" Royce asked. "It's not like he invented breathing."

"Because he figured out the sequence," Jasmine said. "Citrate goes in, gets rearranged, carbons come off as carbon dioxide, and it regenerates. It's a cycle, it comes back around." She pointed at the compost bins, where Ms. Das was turning the pile with a fork, dark steam rising off it in the cool air. "Like that. Things go in, break down, energy comes out, and what's left feeds the next round."

Ms. Das had apparently been listening, because she rested the fork against the bin and came over, wiping her gloves on her jeans. "Did I hear you say Krebs?"

Jasmine, who privately believed she had an excellent memory and had said so at dinner on more than one occasion, said, "Krebs and Johnson, 1937. Nobel Prize."

"He fled Germany," Ms. Das said. "Before that. He was Jewish and he lost his position in 1933 and left." She looked at the dirt diagram. "The prize came later, and he shared it. You said that part right."

"It was shared," Jasmine said. "1953. Physiology or Medicine." She repeated it because repeating it made her feel like someone who knew things, and also, she was beginning to admit, because she wanted to check whether it still sounded true. It did, mostly. The 1937 part she had said once and could not now verify against anything but itself.

Angelina flipped to a fresh page. "Okay, so the cycle makes NADH and FADH2, and those go to the inner membrane, and that's where most of the ATP actually comes from. The electron transport chain. Protons get pumped across, and then they flow back through this enzyme, ATP synthase." She drew a circle in the membrane and labeled it. "Like water through a turbine."

"The putative turbine," Royce said, and Angelina threw a clementine peel at him.

"It's not putative, it's actual. Look at your own notes."

"I don't have notes. I have your notes, photocopied."

Jasmine took the stick and drew arrows between Angelina's membrane drawing and her own dirt bean, connecting the pyruvate to the cycle to the chain, and then, after a moment, drew one more arrow from the whole thing back out to the compost pile. It wasn't in the textbook. But she sat back and looked at it, the glucose from last summer's tomato plants going into the soil, being broken down, being built again into next year's beans, and she thought that Krebs must have felt something when the pieces finally closed into a circle, though she couldn't know that, and said so.

"What I still can't do," she said, "is the order of the intermediates. Succinate, fumarate, malate. I might have that backwards."

"Then you didn't have it handled," Angelina said.

"I have it ninety percent handled." Jasmine erased the bean with the side of her hand and drew it again, ridges and all, no smiley face this time. "Give me the clementines. I'm going to teach it to the compost."

activity: the language of contracts and forms, such as terms, conditions, liability, consent and signatures
knowledge_domain: the language of contracts and forms, such as terms, conditions, liability, consent and signatures
fact: Informed consent in medicine means a patient agrees to treatment after being told its risks, benefits and alternatives in words they can understand.
story:
Dylan found the email at 4:40 on a Tuesday, sandwiched between a furniture ad and a reminder that his library card was about to expire. Please review and sign the attached forms prior to your procedure, it said, addressed to his mother, whose laptop he was borrowing because his own had died a recalcitrant death that involved a spinning wheel and three days of pleading. There were eleven pages. Page one was headed Terms and Conditions of Care. Page nine was a consent form with a signature line at the bottom, thin and expectant, like a held breath.

He skimmed. The document used the word "liability" eleven times, which he counted, because counting felt like doing something. It said the clinic was not liable for outcomes "inherent in the procedure," a phrase so smooth it could slide off a table. It said his mother acknowledged she had been informed of "material risks." It did not, as far as Dylan could tell, say what the risks were.

He texted Karlee, whose father was a paralegal and who therefore spoke fluent fine print. Karlee wrote back within a minute: "consent forms are mostly chicanery with a signature line. they exist so you can't sue later. also hi." Then, after a pause: "unless they didn't actually tell her anything. then it's different."

His mother was in the kitchen marinating chicken, and she waved him off before he finished his first sentence. "The surgeon explained it all at the appointment," she said. "I signed something there already. This is just the rest of it."

"But what did he tell you? Did he say what could go wrong?"

"Dylan." She said his name the way other people say a closing door. "He's a professional. He wouldn't pathologize a routine thing like this, and I'm not going to insult him by asking him to defend it."

He took the laptop to his room, where the radiator ticked and the window let in the smell of someone else's dinner, and opened the clinic's website. Under Patient Rights there was a paragraph about informed consent. He read it twice. Then he read it aloud, quietly, as if the words might change pronunciation between passes.

In the kitchen, his mother's phone buzzed against the counter, and she wiped her hands on the towel before she answered. It was the clinic, a nurse from the pre-op line, confirming her appointment. She said yes, yes, eleven o'clock, yes, fasting after midnight, she knew all of this, she had done this before, with his father, three years ago, and that had been fine.

"There's one thing," she said finally, because Dylan was standing in the doorway holding the laptop open like a hymnal. "My son has been reading the forms. He wants to know about the risks. The specific ones." She turned the phone to speaker without being asked, which was its own small event, and Dylan stepped closer, close enough to smell the ginger on her hands.

"Of course," the nurse said. "That's informed consent. You agree to the treatment after we've told you the risks, the benefits, and the alternatives, in words you can understand. That's the whole point. You're allowed to ask."

"The form doesn't say what the risks are," Dylan said.

"No, the form just records that the conversation happened. The conversation is supposed to happen with a person. If nobody's had it with you yet, then we'll have it now, or the surgeon will before anything starts. You don't sign until you know what you're signing." The nurse's voice had the patience of someone who had explained this many times and still found it worth explaining. "Do you want me to go through them?"

His mother looked at the chicken, then at the phone, then at the ceiling, in that order. "Go ahead," she said.

The nurse talked for eight minutes. Some of it was boring, which Dylan suspected was a mercy, and some of it wasn't. She used the word "alternative" three times, once about doing nothing at all and watching it, which Dylan hadn't known was allowed to count as an option. His mother asked two questions. The second one, about the anesthesia, she asked in a voice half an octave lower than the first.

When the call ended, his mother took the laptop, found the signature line on page nine, and held her finger above the trackpad without pressing. "Don't look so pleased with yourself," she said. Then she scrolled back to page one and started reading.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: Deliberate practice means working on specific weaknesses with a clear goal and immediate feedback, which improves skill more than simply playing through pieces already known.
story:
Victor had come to his grandfather's house every Sunday for three weeks now, and he had told no one, least of all his mother, because the accordion was his inheritance and his business alone. That was how he preferred things. He was not sentimental, and he did not need anyone hovering around while he figured out the instrument on his own, the way his grandfather had figured out carpentry, plumbing, everything, without a single lesson.

The accordion smelled of the closet it had lived in for eleven years, and its bellows leaked a thin wheeze on the push. Victor could already play the opening eight bars of "Blue Skirts" all the way through, no mistakes, because those bars were easy and because his grandfather had whistled them constantly, in the kitchen, on the porch, in the hospital hallway the last October. Victor played those eight bars now, again, then again, and the sound filled the living room where the furniture had not been moved since June.

Mr. Krause from next door let himself in through the back door without knocking, which was a habit Victor claimed to resent and did not. "Heard you from the fence," Mr. Krause said. He was carrying a plate of something wrapped in foil, which he set on the counter as though he happened to be dropping it off anyway. He stood in the doorway and listened to the eight bars one more time. "Play me the middle part," he said. "Bars nine and ten."

"I haven't got there yet."

"So go get them."

Victor played bars nine and ten, and they collapsed. His left hand forgot which button it owned; the bellows ran out of air mid-phrase; a wrong note sat in the room like a spilled glass. He started over at bar one, and Mr. Krause raised a hand, mild, almost apologetic. "No. Not the beginning again. You're not being graded on the beginning." He pulled a chair over and sat. "Your grandfather used to call it deliberate practice. You take the two bars you can't do, you set a goal for them, and I tell you right away what went wrong. That builds more than playing what you already know all afternoon."

"That sounds parochial," Victor said, meaning it sounded small, a thing invented on one porch for one old man.

"It is small," Mr. Krause said. "Two bars. Go."

So Victor worked the two bars, and it was worse than the beginning ever was, because the beginning had let him feel competent and this did not. Mr. Krause listened and said "left hand early" the instant it happened, and "you're rushing, breathe with the bellows," and once, after a take that surprised them both, nothing at all, which Victor understood to mean it had been right. The feedback came fast enough that he could feel each mistake while it was still happening, in his fingers, not afterward in his memory.

At school on Monday, Camelia caught him in the hallway with his earbuds in, listening to a recording of "Blue Skirts" played by someone with an entire orchestra behind him. "You're doing that accordion thing still," she said, not a question. Kalen, beside her, was already halfway into a story about the debate team, about how their coach kept insisting a speech needed more logos and less pathos, and Victor half-listened while Camelia asked how the playing was going. "Fine," he said. "It's fine." He told her the whole song was basically learned. He even believed it as he said it, and that was the strange part, how easily the sentence arrived.

But Sunday came, and he went back, and he knew before he opened the case that the whole song was not basically learned, that it was two good bars and a long slope downward. He played bars nine and ten for Mr. Krause forty times, and somewhere in the middle of those repetitions, something in his left hand stopped being a decision and became a motion. He tried to introspect about it, to catch the exact moment the switch happened, and could not; the learning had gone in below the level where he could watch it, like grief, he supposed, though he would not have said that aloud.

His mother found out the way mothers find out, which is to say she had known for two weeks and had driven past the house twice on her way to nowhere in particular. She came in the back door with groceries she claimed were "just extras," and stood in the living room while he played the two hard bars, then the eight easy ones, then, wobbling but arriving, the whole first half of "Blue Skirts" stitched together. She did not cry, and neither did he, and the three of them knew both of those statements were false in the comfortable way that Sunday afternoons allow.

At the end, Victor asked Mr. Krause whether his grandfather had really left the accordion to him, specifically, in words. Mr. Krause folded his hands and looked at the window for a while. "He left it in the closet," he said. "And he left you with Sundays free. I'd call that specific enough."

Victor fastened the clasps on the case. "Same time next week?"

"Same time," Mr. Krause said, picking up his empty plate. "Bars eleven and twelve."

activity: getting a first part-time job
knowledge_domain: getting a first part-time job
fact: In the United States, every new employee must complete Section 1 of Form I-9, which verifies identity and permission to work, no later than their first day of paid work.
story:
The aquatics centre smelled of chlorine and burnt coffee, and Mathis stood at the front desk in the same shirt he had worn to his interview, holding a clipboard he did not know how to fill out. The manager, a broad woman with a whistle around her neck, had said only, "Section 1, top part, before you hit the water today," and then walked off toward the deep end, where a class of small children thrashed like startled frogs.

Mathis turned the clipboard over. The form was called an I-9, and the top part wanted his full legal name, his address, whether he was a citizen or a permanent resident or something else, and a signature attesting that everything he wrote was true. Below that, Section 2 sat empty, waiting for documents he had not brought because he had not known documents were part of the deal. He had brought a towel, a water bottle, and forty dollars of his own money for the lifeguard certification he was supposed to start paying off out of his first paycheque.

Tabitha was already at the other end of the desk, filling out her own clipboard with the ease of someone who had done paperwork before, because her mother worked at a bank and forms were a kind of family dialect. "You look like you're defusing something," she said without looking up.

"I don't know what any of this is." He held the clipboard out to her like evidence. "She just said Section 1, today, like I was supposed to already know."

Tabitha glanced at the manager, then lowered her voice. "Everybody does it on or before their first day of paid work. My brother got sent home from the grocery store last summer because he showed up without finishing it. He had to come back the next morning before his shift, before they'd pay him for anything." She tapped the top of his form. "So the answer is, yes, right now, before you get in the water."

Mathis read the attestation line twice. It was strange to swear, under penalty of law, to facts about himself that he had never had to think of as facts. He printed his name in the boxes, one letter per box, and his hand felt clumsy, the way it had in third grade when they were learning cursive. When he got to the part asking his status, he paused. His father had come over on a visa years before Mathis was born, and though Mathis had been born here and never questioned it, the form's careful categories made the ground feel briefly less solid, as if citizenship were a tile you could tap to see whether it was loose underneath.

His phone buzzed against his hip. It was a message from Ariella, who had wanted this same job and not gotten it: "Tell me everything. Is the manager terrifying? Did they make you sign your life away yet? Because that's what they do to you at your first job, they make you sign things until you feel like you belong to them." He typed back, "Signed something called an I-9. Had to finish section 1 today, apparently that's the rule, first day of paid work at the latest. So yes, signing my life away. Also I get a whistle." Her reply was a single thumbs-up, which he found oddly noncommittal for someone who had spent June insisting she would rather work at the pool than anywhere on earth.

He finished the form and carried it to the manager, who was now leaning over the edge of the pool, cajoling a shrieking six-year-old into putting his face in the water. "Come on, buddy, one blow, one bubble, you'll be a fish by August," she was saying, her voice all warmth where her clipboard voice had been flat. When Mathis held out the form she checked it against the light, signed something, and said, "Documents for Section 2 by Friday. ID and something with your birth date on it. Don't lose that. People lose that." Then she pointed at the tall chair at the shallow end. "Watch the water until your shift on the certification class starts. If someone goes under, you whistle, you don't go in. That's next week's lesson."

He climbed the chair. From up there the pool resolved into geometry, the painted lane lines running straight under the chop, and the children became small and manageable, each one visible, each splash trackable. He understood suddenly why the manager had wanted the form done first, before any of this. The whole arrangement depended on things being true and on file, on his name being attachable to him, on permission existing somewhere in writing. He had always thought of a job as mostly physiology, as strength and breath and the long underwater swims his father made him do at the lake, saying a lifeguard is made in the lungs. It had not occurred to him that a job was also made of paper.

His father would say something about that tonight, probably. His father believed in paperwork the way some people believed in weather, as a thing you could not argue with, and Mathis had spent the spring arguing with him anyway, insisting he could start work without the certification, without the forms, without the waiting. His father had refused to drive him to interviews until school ended, and Mathis had gone on his bike, in the rain, mostly out of spite. Now, from the tall chair, the spite seemed smaller than it had at the time, though he still was not sure his father had been right to slow him down, or only right by accident, the way a stopped clock is.

A boy in orange trunks ducked under the rope into the deep end, and Mathis leaned forward, one hand drifting toward the whistle around his own neck, new and cold, not yet his. The manager looked up from the six-year-old, saw Mathis watching, and gave him a single nod. Then she cupped her hands around her mouth and called across the chlorine haze, "You. Boy in the orange. Back behind the rope."

activity: to use a geographic information system to overlay flood risk and housing on a city map
knowledge_domain: to use a geographic information system to overlay flood risk and housing on a city map
fact: Landscape architect Ian McHarg's 1969 book Design with Nature promoted stacking maps of soil, water and other factors to decide land use, an idea that GIS later automated.
story:
Maelie had the laptop open on the kitchen table, the city map rendered in pale layers beneath her cursor, when her mother called from the hallway that the boxes from Grandpa's had arrived and were she going to help or just sit there. She sat there a minute longer. The GIS software belonged to Ms. Kamau's seminar, and the assignment belonged to Maelie: overlay flood risk and housing and see what the city had built where it should not have. She had clicked the flood layer on and off twice, watching the blue creep up the river streets, before she went to the hallway and started cutting tape.

The boxes smelled of pencil shavings and old paper. Inside the second one, nested between a browned photograph and a protractor, she found tracing paper. Dozens of sheets, each drawn in faded ink: soil, one said in her grandfather's slanted hand. Water. Slope. Woodland. She lifted the soil sheet and held it to the ceiling light, and the hatch marks floated translucent over nothing. She set it down on the water sheet, and where the two darkened together, the land seemed to say something. Her mother leaned in the doorway drying a cup. "He did those for the county," she said. "Before computers did it for anyone." Maelie laid the slope sheet on top and the city appeared in her mind unbidden, all its wet and unsuitable places suddenly legible.

I kept stacking, sheet over sheet, until the pile was an inch thick and the composite underneath had gone nearly black where everything agreed. It was strange to hold a decision in my hands, a whole argument about land use compressed into translucent pages. I thought of the seminar reading, the paperback Ms. Kamau had left on the shelf: Ian McHarg, Design with Nature, 1969. He had promoted stacking maps of soil, water, and other factors to decide land use. I hadn't understood, at first, what that meant, but my grandfather's kitchen-table method had apparently traveled from hand to machine, because the whole idea was what GIS later automated. The software on my laptop was this pile of paper, only faster, and more patient.

She texted Summer a photograph of the stack, angled so the layers showed. "is that ur grandpa's," Summer wrote back, then, "wait those are like the layers we did in class." Maelie typed yes and then deleted it, because it wasn't quite like. The software let her slide a slider and watch the hundred-year floodplain swallow a block of rentals; the paper only sat there, mute and decided. Ashley, when she came over that evening with her bookbag still on, crouched over the sheets and said, "So he'd put soil over water and just, what, squint?" "Stack them," Maelie said. "Soil, water, whatever else. Then you know where to build." Ashley frowned at the darkest composite area. "And they built there anyway."

They did. That was the finding, and Maelie had it in a table now: the flood layer crossed the housing layer, and the intersection was not scattered. It concentrated in the low-rent flats by the creek, the ones whose parking lot she had skated across in middle school without knowing the water remembered that ground. She worked until ten, then past ten, dragging transparency sliders, exporting maps. Her mother brought tea to allay the worry she seemed to feel about something, though Maelie could not tell what; maybe the late hour, maybe the photograph of Grandpa that had surfaced from the third box, young and holding a surveyor's rod like an igneous seam of certainty running through softer rock.

At the seminar the next afternoon, Ms. Kamau had them present in pairs. Ashley went first and was brisk and certain: here is the floodplain, here is the housing, here is the injustice, the conclusion wrote itself. When it was Maelie's turn, she put up two images side by side, the exported map and the photograph of the stacked tracing paper. She said the software was the paper, automated, one practice descending from the other. Then she said the thing that had kept her up. "The map can tell you where not to build," she said. "It can't tell you why anyone built there anyway, or what you say to the people living in the dark part of the composite now. I keep thinking the map is an answer, and then I think it's only a question with better lighting."

Ms. Kamau asked whether that made the analysis useless. Maelie turned the question over and did not hurry it. "No," she said. "It makes it a beginning. If we pretend it's the whole argument, we're standing in a quagmire and calling it a floor. But we still know where the water goes. We know that part for sure." She looked at the two images, the paper and the software, sixty years apart and saying the same thing in different hands. Summer caught her eye from the second row and mouthed, good one. Maelie clicked to the final slide, the one she had made at midnight, both layers merged over the flats by the creek, the blue rising through the rooftops like something patient. She left it up and did not say anything more.

activity: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
knowledge_domain: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
fact: Progressive overload means gradually increasing training demands, such as weight, distance or intensity, so the body keeps having a reason to adapt.
story:
The gym smelled of rubber and cold metal on the morning Brianna taped the sheet to the wall beside the squat rack. She had ruled it into seven columns, one for each day, and she had left two of them deliberately blank. Rest, she had written in Monday's box, and then, feeling extravagant, rest again on Thursday. Coach had assigned the project to anyone who wanted a spot on the training committee for spring season, and Brianna wanted it badly enough that she had stayed up past midnight with a calculator and a handout about warm-up sequences, deciding who would jog, who would stretch, who would lift.

Arnaud found her there before first period, a towel around his neck, already sweating. He had been coming to the gym since September, and he went at it with a devotion that made her feel lazy by comparison. Same bench press, same weight, same ten reps. Same chin-ups, same count. She watched him settle onto the bench and rack the bar, and she noticed, not for the first time, that his numbers never changed. He had told her once, almost proudly, that he had done the identical workout every weekday for four months.

"You wrote rest on two days," he said, squinting at her chart. "That's wasteful."

"That's the point of a plan. Warm-ups too. You never warm up."

"I don't need it. I do the same thing every day, so nothing surprises my body." He said it like a law of physics, and she didn't argue, because she was still deciding what she believed. Her philosophy elective had spent a week on epistemology, on how you could know a thing was true rather than merely familiar, and she had liked the question more than any of the answers. Arnaud knew his routine the way you knew your own bedroom in the dark. Whether it was getting him anywhere was a different matter.

She spent the week filling in the rest of her chart. On Tuesday she penciled in heavier dumbbells than the week before, and on Friday heavier again, and she wrote a small arrow in the margin, up and to the right. Hajar leaned over her shoulder in the bleachers during assembly, her diaphanous scarf thrown back, and read the arrow and the words beside it.

"Progressive overload," Hajar said, tapping the term. "That's what the handout calls it."

"Which means what, exactly?"

"You keep nudging the weight up. Or the distance, or how hard you go. A little at a time, so your body always has a reason to keep adapting." Hajar shrugged. "It's on page three."

Brianna looked across the gym at Arnaud, who was midway through his ten bench presses, the same ten at the same weight as yesterday and the day before and every day since September, and something assembled itself in her mind with an almost audible click. She thought of her own track times, stalled for a month at the same pace, and she had blamed the weather, the track surface, her shoes. She had never once considered that she had given her body the same demand until it had quietly finished meeting it.

From Arnaud's angle on the bench, the ceiling tiles were the familiar grid he counted his reps against, and the bar came down and went up as it always did. He saw Brianna crossing the gym toward him with her chart in one hand, and he noticed, because he noticed her more than he would have admitted, that she was limping very slightly, favoring her left knee on the turns. She had been limping, he realized, since at least last week, maybe longer, hidden under long warm-up pants and a steady smile. She reached the rack and set her chart on the floor beside his water bottle.

"Arnaud, I think I know why your numbers haven't moved since fall."

He racked the bar and sat up, breathing hard, forearms slick. "Go on."

"You ask your body for the same thing every single day. Same weight, same reps. It adapted, and then it stopped, because you stopped asking for anything more. If you went up a little, week by week..."

"Or the distance," she added, and then she stopped, because he was looking at her knee, at the way she was keeping her weight off it.

"How long," he said quietly, "has that been hurting?"

"Since the time trials." She looked down at her chart, at the two honest rest days she had defended so confidently that morning, and understood suddenly that she had planned them for bodies that obeyed diagrams. "I kept adding intensity every week because the plan said to. Maybe I added it wrong. Maybe I needed the rest more than the work."

"Monday's box still says rest," Arnaud said, and tapped the paper with two fingers. "I'll be here. You should probably be somewhere else."

activity: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
knowledge_domain: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
fact: Josef Albers made over 1,000 works in his Homage to the Square series from 1950 until 1976, keeping nested squares constant while changing only the colours.
story:
The assignment sheet said ten artworks, one theme, one artist's statement, due in spring, and Sebastian had taped it above his desk in September like a dare. By October he had three paintings that had nothing to do with each other: a football helmet, his grandfather's hands, and a lake so blue it looked like toothpaste. Mr. Becker circled nothing on the sheet, which was somehow worse than circling something. "Right now you have ten directions," he said in the hallway, already walking away. "I need one."

Nya had solved the problem by deciding she was, in her own words, "the portrait girl." Ten faces, charcoal and white chalk, every one of them somebody from their lunch table. She wanted the portfolio to be so unified that the reviewers at the art school in Chicago would see it and think of her instantly, one name, one style. She had already made Keeley sit for forty minutes under the science wing's fluorescent lights because, she said, "they make you look like an interesting corpse." Keeley had held still out of friendship and complained the whole time.

Sebastian tried themes the way other people try diets. Doors, for a week. Then birds, then grief, which lasted two days because it turned out he wasn't grieving anything and the paintings were lies. In the library, hiding from his own sketchbook, he found a shelf of art books nobody touched and pulled down a fat orange one because the cover was ten nested squares, all different colors, like a target melting. Inside there were pages and pages of the same thing: squares inside squares inside squares, gray and rust and violet, green against a red so close to blood it made his teeth ache.

Nya found him there at lunch, flipping. "That's Albers," she said, leaning over his shoulder. "Homage to the Square. He made over a thousand of them, from 1950 until 1976, and the nested squares never change. Only the colors change." She tapped a pale one, all winter grays. "My mom has a print. It's the boreal one, we call it. Looks like February in the UP." Sebastian stared at the grid of images, the same bones wearing a hundred different skins, and felt something shift in his chest like a stuck drawer finally sliding open.

The problem was that Nya thought it was a terrible idea for him. "A thousand of them, and he's a famous modernist with a whole movement behind him," she said in the studio after school, arms crossed over her smock. "You'd be a teenager with ten copies of one painting." She was arguing for her own reasons, and Sebastian knew it, because if his portfolio worked, the portrait girl thing stopped being the only smart approach in the room. Keeley, gluing bottle caps to a canvas for reasons nobody questioned, said, "At least his would match." Keeley wanted, more than anything, for the three of them to still be friends in June, and had appointed herself diplomat accordingly.

So Sebastian started small, which was the part he'd always skipped. He cut a stencil, one square inside another inside another, and spent a Saturday painting it nine times on nine small boards. The first four were experiments he'd subsume later into the series, or that was the word Mr. Becker used when he walked past and looked, hands in pockets, saying nothing for a long moment. The fifth board was a mistake: he'd meant olive green and mixed something like dried mustard, and when he put the brown-gray beside it, the gray turned cold and the mustard turned warm, and neither color had actually changed at all. He sat back on his stool like a person hearing a rumor about himself that happened to be true.

He learned the subtlety the hard way, board by board. Two colors that looked nothing alike alone could become nearly twins with the right border between them. He started keeping notes on the backs, tiny and obsessive, like a man leaving messages for the version of himself who would paint tomorrow. When Nya finally came over and stood in front of the row of nine, her arms uncrossed by themselves. "Okay," she said. "The third one is doing something to the fourth one that I don't understand, and it's making me angry, and I want to learn how." It was, from Nya, practically a standing ovation. They spent the rest of the afternoon arguing about warm grays, and Keeley read a magazine nearby and occasionally said "agree to disagree," which settled nothing and kept the peace.

Sebastian still didn't know what his artist's statement would say. He didn't know if one element changing was a theme or just a trick, whether he was paying homage or hiding, whether the reviewers would see patience or a kid who couldn't draw anything but squares. He wrote a draft that read like a hostage note and threw it away. But on Monday morning he set up the tenth board, laid out the colors he'd mixed the night before, the gray like a February sky and the red that made his teeth ache, and pressed the stencil down flat with the heel of his hand.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: Robert Cialdini's 1976 study found that students wore more university clothing after their football team won and said 'we' more when describing wins than losses.
story:
The game had come down to a field goal, forty-two yards, and Emily was the only person in the living room sitting down. Her father was on his feet, her uncle was gripping the mantel, and Mederick, who had arrived an hour earlier with chips and an opinion about the secondary, had both hands pressed to his head as if holding his skull together. Briana sat cross-legged on the rug, quiet the way she got when she cared about something and didn't want anyone to know.

The kick went up, wobbled, and cleared the crossbar with what looked like inches to spare. The room detonated. Her father hugged the uncle; the uncle hugged a lamp. Mederick screamed, "We won, we actually won," and then, as though remembering himself, laughed and said it again, quieter, "I mean, they won. Whatever. We won."

Emily stayed on the couch, holding her lukewarm soda, watching him. Three weeks ago the same team had lost in overtime, and she remembered exactly what Mederick had said then, because she had written it down in the margin of her psychology notes. He had said, "They couldn't stop the run," with a small shrug, and then changed the subject to a girl in his Spanish class. She had written it down because of Mr. Harper.

Mr. Harper taught her psychology class, and on the day before the big game he had told them almost nothing, which was his method. He had put a question on the board: after a win, whose clothes do you wear? Emily had guessed nobody's, and he had said no, and told them to look it up for themselves, that the answer was from 1976, a study by a man named Robert Cialdini. She had found it that night at her desk, and it had felt like being handed a pair of x-ray glasses. Students wore more university clothing after their football team won. And when they described the games, they said "we" more for wins than for losses. Wins belonged to them. Losses belonged to somebody else.

Now Mederick was doing it, live, in her living room, wearing the university sweatshirt he had bought in September and never once put on before today. She felt a strange double feeling: the pleasure of watching a theory work in the wild, and something colder underneath, because if it worked on him it probably worked on her too. She was wearing her own team shirt. She had put it on before the game without thinking, which was precisely the problem.

"Can I ask you something?" she said, when the shouting thinned out. "What did you say when they lost three weeks ago?"

Mederick tore open the chips. "I don't remember. Something like, they got exposed."

"So 'they' for a loss and 'we' for a win."

Briana looked up from the rug. Mederick's hand stopped in the bag.

"That's from a study," Emily said. "Robert Cialdini, 1976. After their football team won, students wore more university clothing. And they said 'we' more describing wins than losses." She hadn't meant to recite it, but it came out in the flat, careful voice she used when she was nervous of being right.

Mederick chewed. "So you're saying I don't actually care about the team."

"I'm saying you're a data point."

Briana laughed, one short note, then covered it. "He's allowed to be happy," she said. "You don't have to historicize everything, Em." Briana used words like that when she wanted to end an argument rather than win it, and it usually worked, because it made Emily feel small and bookish, the parochial girl who thought a footnote was a personality.

Emily let it sit for a minute. Her father and the uncle were replaying the kick in miniature, one of them snapping an imaginary ball. The room was warm and full, and Mederick was grinning at the television, and the sweatshirt was genuinely, stupidly happy on him.

"Okay," Emily said. "Both things, then. It's real happiness and it's borrowed. I don't know where one stops." She turned the soda can in her hands. "I'm not even sure I'm outside it. I put this shirt on without deciding to."

"Then we're all in the oligarchy of the winning," Mederick said, gesturing grandly at the room, and it was the wrong word, and Briana told him so, and he argued that in his living room, tonight, it meant whoever gets to say 'we.'

Her father called from beside the television that they were showing the stands, so Emily stood, finally, and came to the edge of the crowd of them. On the screen, thousands of people in university colors were hugging strangers, and she caught herself thinking, without any distance at all, "Look what we did."

activity: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
knowledge_domain: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
fact: India has marked voters' fingers with indelible ink based on silver nitrate since its 1962 general election, so no one can vote twice.
story:
Henry's ballot arrived in the mail on a Tuesday, folded inside a manila envelope he almost threw away with the pizza flyers. He carried it to the kitchen table and set it down beside his phone, where Lilah had just sent a photo from her gap year: her aunt in Chennai, grinning, holding up a purple-stained thumb.

"Hasn't washed off in four days," Lilah had captioned it. "She's so proud."

Henry studied the image while eating cereal. His own ballot sat untouched, and the difference bothered him in a way he couldn't quite name. His grandmother in Chennai had waited in the sun for hours, and what she got to keep was a mark. He got a privacy envelope and a return label.

When Lane came over that evening to work on their shared physics problem set, Henry showed him the photo. Lane leaned across the table, headphones still around his neck.

"Oh, that's the ink," Lane said. "My dad's from Mumbai. He says it's indelible, based on silver nitrate. They've marked voters' fingers with it since the 1962 general election, so no one can vote twice." He said it the way he recited batting averages, matter-of-fact, then stole a handful of Henry's chips.

"Since 1962," Henry repeated. He did the arithmetic without meaning to. His grandmother had been younger than he was now. Everyone in that country, every election, carrying proof on their hands.

"You're weirdly fascinated," Lane said.

"I'm voting for the first time on Saturday. I turned eighteen last month." Henry picked up the manila envelope, turned it over, put it down again. "And nobody will know. There's no mark, no line, no proof I did anything."

"So vote and move on. That's the whole point of privacy." Lane gesticulated at the envelope with his chip, scattering crumbs. "You want someone watching you? That's the opposite of how it works here."

"Privacy isn't the only value, though. My grandmother shows her finger to everyone. She's not showing who she voted for. She's showing that she voted."

Lane rolled his eyes, but not unkindly. "You sound like a documentary."

After Lane left, Henry's mother came through the kitchen and paused at the table, where the ballot and his phone still lay side by side, Lilah's aunt grinning between them.

"Are you going to fill that out or frame it?" she asked.

"Both, maybe." He turned the phone toward her. "In India they mark your finger with this ink. Silver nitrate. It doesn't come off. Since 1962."

"I know," she said. "Your great-uncle used to gesticulate with that finger for a week after every election, like he'd been knighted." She smiled at some picture only she could see, then became practical again. "The polls open at seven on Saturday. I'll drive you before work if you want."
