He sat with the ballot after she went upstairs. Lane thought the secret ballot was the whole achievement, and Henry could see the shape of that argument: that a vote you couldn't be punished or bribed for was a vote you actually owned. But his grandmother's ink finger said something else, that there was a public part of citizenship too, a visible counting of yourself among the counted. He wondered whether a person needed both, or whether wanting both made him some kind of egoist, collecting proofs of his own virtue. Maybe, he thought, the ink was for a country that had to worry about people voting twice, and the envelope was for a country that trusted its lists. Or maybe it was simpler than that. He didn't know, and he noticed that not knowing felt less like failure than he'd expected. It felt like the beginning of paying attention.

He filled out the ballot at the kitchen table, sliding it into the privacy envelope slowly, the way his grandmother would have wanted a ceremony conducted. He would still go to the polling place on Saturday with his mother, because he'd said he would, because the machine would ding him as having returned his mail ballot and that small public fact pleased him.

Then he texted Lilah: tell your aunt I voted my first time too. No ink, but still.

Lilah sent back a single purple thumb emoji, and, a minute later, a photograph of her own hand holding a pen over an absentee form, tongue out in concentration.

He set his phone face-up beside the sealed envelope and left them there together on the table.

activity: to use a geographic information system to overlay flood risk and housing on a city map
knowledge_domain: to use a geographic information system to overlay flood risk and housing on a city map
fact: GIS data comes in two main forms: vector data uses points, lines and polygons, while raster data is a grid of cells, each holding one value.
story:
The travel agency had one working computer in the back, between the poster of Santorini and the shelf of brochures for cruises nobody booked anymore, and Ms. Szabó let Eli use it on Thursdays after he swept and alphabetized the Caribbean rack. This arrangement suited everyone. Ms. Szabó got a swept floor, Eli got a machine faster than the laptop at home, and the agency got the faint impression of being part of the digital age. Eli was not, despite what he told his mother, working on college applications back there. He was building a map.

The map was his own idea, which he was proud of, and also the reason he hadn't told anyone except Elliana. He wanted to lay the city's flood zones over its housing stock, both maps downloaded free from the county website, so he could see which streets his aunt's neighborhood sat on and whether the city's plan to widen the creek would put water where people lived. It was the kind of project that sounded noble when he described it, and he described it often, usually beginning with the words "somebody has to."

The problem appeared on the second Thursday. The housing map loaded as tidy shapes, parcels drawn like stained glass, each one clickable, each one with an address attached. The flood map loaded as something else entirely, a haze of pixels like a photo of weather. When he stacked them, the haze sat on top of the shapes like fog over a parking lot, and he couldn't click anything, couldn't select a street, couldn't even tell where one flood zone ended and another began. He restarted the computer, which fixed nothing, which surprised no one except him.

He texted Elliana from the front counter while Ms. Szabó explained to a customer, for the third time that month, that there were no direct flights to Budapest in February.

ELI: the flood map is broken. it's just pixels.
ELLIANA: it's not broken, it's raster.
ELI: what
ELLIANA: raster data is a grid of cells and every cell holds one value. like a photo. your housing map is vector, it uses points lines and polygons.
ELI: how do you know this
ELLIANA: my dad does surveying. also you could just google it
ELI: I don't need to google it, I have you

Eli read the message twice. Somewhere in there was the whole shape of his problem, though it took him another twenty minutes and a second text, the one where Elliana wrote "the computer isn't confused, YOU'RE confused," for him to see it. The two maps weren't broken. They were two different languages describing the same city. The shapes spoke in boundaries and ownership. The pixels spoke in elevation and water, one cell at a time, each cell carrying a single value like a grain of rice in its own square of the grid.

The solution, once he understood the problem, was almost insultingly small. The software had a tool that drew a line around all the cells above a certain value, converting the fog into a polygon, and when he dragged the new shape over the parcels, the map did the thing he had wanted it to do all along. His aunt's street lit up orange. Half the cul-de-sac, all of the lots backing onto the creek, the exact houses he'd delivered newspapers to for two years. He sat back in Ms. Szabó's swivel chair and looked at it for a long time.

There was a complication, and he was honest enough with himself to admit it, though not honest enough to tell Elliana. His own house, the one his parents had spent fifteen years paying for, sat just inside the orange. Not deep in it, not the worst of it, but inside. If he screenshotted the map and sent it to the neighborhood association, as he'd been planning, as he'd drafted the email in his head during chemistry, his mother would see it too. She had inured herself to the creek the way people inure themselves to any slow risk, by deciding every spring that the water in the street was normal, that the sump pump was just loud, that the insurance assessment was a formality. Eli had done the same thing, if he was being fair, which he usually wasn't. His project was supposed to be about other people's streets. He had not counted on complicity arriving by screenshot.

He printed the map on the agency's color printer, which Ms. Szabó noticed, because Ms. Szabó noticed everything and mentioned approximately forty percent of it. She came back while the page was still warm and set down two cups of tea she hadn't been asked for.

"Better than the brochures," she said, looking at the orange. "What is it?"

"The creek project. Which streets flood and who lives on them."

She studied it. "This one here." Her finger rested on a parcel near the bottom, near the senior building where she'd lived before moving above the shop. "That is water or that is people?"

"Both," Eli said. "That's kind of the point."

She sipped her tea. Outside, the customer who didn't want February in Budapest was unlocking a bicycle with a sullen, defeated slowness, as though the airline schedules were a personal insult. Ms. Szabó watched him through the glass.

"So what will you do with it," she said. It wasn't quite a question, the way she said it.

"I'm sending it to the neighborhood association." He said it firmly, the way he'd said it to himself, and then heard how firm it sounded and turned the map face down on the counter. "Mostly. There's a part I'm still deciding about."

"The deciding part," Ms. Szabó said, "is usually the map."

She went back to the front, and Eli picked up the page again and looked at the small orange polygon that was his own house, his own window, his own loud sump pump, holding its one value like everything else in the grid. He took out his phone and started typing, then deleted it, then started again.

"Elliana," he said to no one, out loud in the empty back room, "what do you do when the map is right and you wish it wasn't?"

The printer clicked, cooling. He hit send.

activity: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
knowledge_domain: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
fact: A table read is a seated read-through of a script by the cast, used to hear how the dialogue sounds before any staging begins.
story:
Angelina arranged three kitchen chairs in a half circle in the living room, script pages face down on the coffee table, and then rearranged them twice before her friends arrived because the order kept feeling like a verdict. She had written a ten-minute play about the night two years ago when her father, coming home from a double shift, had drifted into a parked truck three streets from their house. Nobody had died. There had been an insurance payout, an indemnity her mother signed for in the hospital cafeteria while Angelina sat beside her holding a paper cup of coffee that went cold untouched. That was the scene she had chosen: the cafeteria, the two of them, the silence.

Younes arrived first, still in his work polo, and Tyson came ten minutes later with the bag of chips he always brought and never opened. She handed them each a copy of the script. "So we just sit and read it," she said. "It's called a table read. A seated read-through by the cast, to hear how the dialogue sounds before any staging begins." Tyson nodded as though this were obvious, but she could tell from his face that he was filing it away, the way he filed away everything before deciding whether to mock it.

They started. Younes read the mother, which Angelina had worried would be funny and which, to his credit, he played straight, leaning forward with the pages in both hands. Tyson read the father, though the father had only six lines, all of them on the phone. Angelina read herself, or the girl she had written, which she was already discovering was not quite the same thing.

The trouble began at line nineteen. "You always say it could have been worse," the daughter says in the script, "and I always know exactly what you mean." Tyson read it flat, the way anyone would read it, and the sentence lay there on the carpet between the chairs like something dropped. Angelina heard it with a strange double exposure: in her memory, in the actual cafeteria, she had said something like that, and her mother had laughed, one syllable, tired. But on the page the line sounded nothing like how people talked. It sounded like a line.

"Keep going," she said, and they did, but she had stopped listening as a writer and started listening as an eavesdropper. Later in the script the mother mentions the record player in the front room, the obsolescent one nobody had fixed since before the accident, and the daughter offers to sell it, and the mother says no. Younes gave that no a small weight she hadn't written into it, and it landed harder than anything she'd typed. She thought about how her father, during the months he spent recuperating on the couch with his leg elevated, had played records on that machine every afternoon, and how her mother had never once complained about the noise.

They finished. Tyson opened his chips at last, which she took as a verdict of some kind. "So," he said, "the mom's the one keeping the record player."

"Obviously," Younes said.

"I'm asking whether she knows that," Tyson said, and Angelina understood he meant the character, and also possibly her mother, and also possibly herself, since the play was supposedly about her own life and she had not known, sitting in that cafeteria two years ago, what she knew now, or thought she knew now. She had written the play to prove something, though she hadn't let herself name what. Maybe that her mother should have made a different choice that year. Maybe that she herself should have said more, in the cafeteria, than nothing.

There was a knock at the door and Mr. Anderson from next door stood on the step holding a parcel that had been left at his house by mistake. He asked, with genuine interest, what the chairs were for, and she said she was workshopping a play, and he wished her luck and went back through the hedge. When she sat down again the room felt different, smaller and warmer, a place where things happened rather than a set she was designing.

She took the pages back from Tyson and Younes and crossed out line nineteen with a pen that almost ran dry. In its place she wrote nothing yet. "I don't know what she actually says," she admitted. "My mom didn't say it could have been worse. She said the coffee was cold." Younes suggested she write that instead, and Tyson said the cold coffee line was better anyway, and she sat looking at the blank space where the sentence had been, pen hovering, unable to decide whether truth made better theatre or worse.

"Read it again from the top," she said, "and this time nobody perform anything," and she turned back to the first page and waited for her own words to become strangers to her one more time.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: For Mexico's Day of the Dead on November 1 and 2, families build home altars called ofrendas with orange marigolds, whose bright color and strong scent are believed to guide souls home.
story:
Sophia's grandmother had been dead for three weeks, and the marigolds were wrong. Her uncle had bought bundles of them at the flower stall that morning, orange as traffic cones, and now her mother was trying to arrange them on the table in Tía Rosa's garage while the aunties argued about whether the sugar skulls went on the top shelf or the middle one. Nobody had built an altar for Abuela before, because Abuela had been alive, and now the family had until tonight, November first, to get it right.

"They're called ofrendas," her cousin said when Sophia stood staring at the half-built tiers of crates and paper. Murray had come along because his own family was out of town and Sophia had promised him tamales. He was hovering near the door with his jacket still on, looking at the photograph of Abuela propped against the wall, unframed, still creased from the envelope it had arrived in decades ago. "My Spanish teacher showed us pictures. For the first and second of November. The flowers guide the spirits home." He said it quickly, half apologetic, as if knowing things about someone else's tradition were a trespass.

Sophia had assumed she would know what to do. She had spent the last three years telling anyone who asked that she was half this and half that, that she didn't really do religion, that the whole thing was culture, not belief, and culture could be picked up like a jacket whenever she wanted it. But Abuela's death had made the jacket heavy. At the funeral she had stood between her father, who cried openly, and her mother, who did not cry at all, and had understood that she belonged to neither posture entirely. She wanted, more than she could say out loud, to place her grandmother's photograph on the altar and feel that it meant something. The deadline pressed on her like a hand on the back of her neck. By midnight tonight, the family said, the souls began to arrive, guided by the marigolds, their bright color and their strong scent showing the way home.

"I don't know if I believe that," she said to Murray, quietly, while her mother wrestled a strand of papel picado above the table.

"You don't have to believe it all at once," he said. "My mom says half of what people believe started out as somebody deciding to do a thing and then finding out why later."

She remembered, then, being nine, in Abuela's kitchen in the summer, the year before the family stopped making the long drive south. Abuela had set a plate of pan dulce on the floor by the back door, and Sophia had asked who it was for, and Abuela had said, "For whoever comes," and laughed, and brushed flour off her apron. At the time Sophia had thought it was for the neighbor's dog. Now she wasn't sure it hadn't been for a dead husband, offered without ceremony, without an altar, without believing anything in particular except that the dead are owed a plate.

Her uncle had begun, in his loud way, to lionize Abuela, telling the room she had been the strongest woman he'd ever known, a saint, a fighter, and Sophia felt her jaw tighten. Abuela had been sharp-tongued and often unfair; she had once not spoken to Sophia's father for a year over a political argument, though she was nobody's demagogue, just stubborn. The aunties nodded along anyway, converting a difficult woman into a monument, and Sophia understood why they needed to, and also why she couldn't. She didn't want the false version. She wanted the one who put bread on the floor and laughed at her own question.

Her mother, meanwhile, wanted nothing said at all. Sophia watched her straighten the marigolds a fourth time, their smell filling the garage, sharp and almost citrusy, the way the whole evening was sharp and almost something else.

"Can I put the photo up?" Sophia asked her.

Her mother's hands stilled. "It's not a photograph contest. You just set it there."

"I mean, is it okay if I do it. Not you."

Her mother looked at her for a long moment, and something in her face shifted, like a door eased open an inch. "Yes," she said. "Set it in the middle. Where the flowers are thick."

The middle shelf was crowded, so Sophia moved the sugar skulls aside and set the creased photograph where the marigolds could lean against it, orange petals brushing Abuela's shoulder, the scent pooling around her face. Behind her, her uncle launched into another story, and her mother, for the first time all afternoon, corrected him: "She hated that song, Beto." Murray caught Sophia's eye across the garage and raised his plate of tamales slightly, an embryonic toast that never quite got said out loud.

Whether anything came home tonight, Sophia could not claim to know, and she was tired of pretending certainty in either direction. She only knew that she had done the thing, with her own hands, and that the wanting had quieted a little, the way a held breath lets itself out. Her mother came to stand beside her, close enough that their arms touched, and said, almost too low to hear over the aunties, "She would have said the flowers are too many."

"Then we take some off tomorrow," Sophia said, and reached for one stem.

activity: to interview for a part-time job with confident eye contact and clear answers
knowledge_domain: to interview for a part-time job with confident eye contact and clear answers
fact: The STAR method structures an interview answer as Situation, Task, Action and Result, so a story about past experience ends with what actually happened.
story:
The job posting had been taped to the door of the coffee place since September, and Faith had walked past it twice a day for a whole semester before she thought, seriously, of answering it. Sixteen felt old enough for a job. Sixteen felt, some mornings, barely old enough to cross the street without narrating it to herself. The application was one page. The interview, the owner said on the phone, would be Saturday at ten, and would take about fifteen minutes.

The problem revealed itself on Wednesday, when she practiced with Oceane in the cafeteria and discovered that she could not answer a single question without drifting. "Tell me about a time you handled a disagreement," Oceane read off her phone, and Faith began with the bake sale, detoured through the weather that weekend, mentioned Zachary's opinions about pricing, and ended somewhere near the concept of fairness in general. Oceane timed it. Four minutes and ten seconds, and she hadn't said what happened at the end.

"You lost me at the tent blowing over," Oceane said. "Did the tent blow over? I don't even know that."

Faith laughed, then stopped laughing, because the interview was in three days and this was apparently how she sounded. After school she went to find Ms. Le, who kept a box of career-center handouts outside her classroom and never asked why anyone wanted one. Faith commandeered the whole interview section and sat on the hallway floor to read it. Most of the pamphlets looked moribund, fonts from another decade, a cover photo of a teenager in a necktie shaking hands with a man in a different necktie. But one sheet, photocopied and slightly crooked, had a little diagram on it. A question about a past experience, the diagram suggested, could be answered in four moves: Situation, Task, Action, Result.

"So it's called the STAR method," Faith said to Oceane the next day, holding up the sheet. "Situation, Task, Action, Result. You tell it like a story, but it ends with what actually happened."

"Like a story with a receipt," Oceane said.

They tried it in the library, in a corner by the windows where the librarian tolerated them. Faith laid the problem out again: Saturday, the coffee place, fifteen minutes, and the fact that her answers wandered. The bake sale question came back, and this time she walked through it deliberately. The situation was the fundraiser, the week before the holiday fair. The task was two dozen volunteers and one cash box and no plan for disagreements. The action was she made a pricing sheet and taped it where everyone could see it. The result was they raised the money and nobody yelled, or at least nobody yelled where Faith could hear it.

"One minute fifty," Oceane said, staring at the timer. "That's, like, half. And I actually know what happened now."

It felt almost too neat. Faith turned the handout over, wondering whether real interviews ran on diagrams. The maxim at the bottom of the sheet said something like "Practice makes prepared," which made her wince, and yet the diagram itself had done something the maxim only gestured at. It had taken a mess she knew how to feel and turned it into something she knew how to say. Was that confidence, she wondered, or just structure wearing confidence as a coat? She wasn't sure those were different things. Maybe confident people had simply built the structure so long ago that they'd forgotten it was there.

Zachary wandered over during their third round and appointed himself the difficult interviewer. "Why do you want this job," he said flatly, not even a question, and Faith caught herself starting to talk about the economy. She stopped. Maybe STAR didn't fit every question. "I want it because I'm here every morning anyway," she said, "and because I make good coffee at home and I'd like to find out if that means anything." Zachary wrote something invisible on his palm and nodded gravely.

The morning of the interview she wore the one blouse without a stain history and arrived at nine fifty. The owner, a woman with flour on one wrist, asked the disagreement question almost exactly as Oceane had, and Faith felt the diagram light up behind her eyes, four little rooms in a row. Situation, task, action, result, and then she was finished, and there was flour-wrist silence, and the silence felt less like failure than like space.

"One more thing," the woman said. "Look at me when you answer. You did it fine that time. Do it every time."

Faith looked at her, directly, and held it longer than was comfortable. "Can I tell you about the tent, too?" she said. "It's not on my application."

activity: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
knowledge_domain: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
fact: The principle called Chekhov's gun, from the playwright Anton Chekhov, holds that anything clearly shown on stage early should matter later in the play.
story:
Hannah taped the last masking paper strip to the gym floor and stepped back to look at the rectangle she had drawn where her kitchen used to be. The bleachers were folded against the wall, the basketball hoops winched up out of sight, and the space still smelled of rubber and floor wax, which was wrong for a kitchen, but Mr. Tesfaye had said the audience would believe whatever the actors believed. Her ten-minute play was about the afternoon her brother came home from the police station the second time, the day her mother put a plate of food in front of him and did not sit down. Hannah had written it in four drafts, and each draft had gotten shorter, and she did not know yet whether that meant it was getting better or getting smaller.

Nico arrived carrying a stack of folding chairs, Kaiden behind with the copy box, and they set up the audience in a shallow arc at the edge of the taped floor. "Table read before we block anything," Hannah said, and handed out pages. She had cast Nico as her brother and Kaiden as her mother, and she would read the stage directions herself, standing at the side with the script she had slept under for a week.

They read it straight through, no stopping, the way Mr. Tesfaye had shown them, and the sound of the words in the gym was different from the sound of the words in her room at midnight. The play opened with her mother at the counter, sealing an envelope, setting it on the fruit bowl, and saying nothing about it. Then the brother came in. Then the plate. Then the silence that Hannah had spent two whole pages trying to write and finally cut to a single line, "They ate like that," which Kaiden delivered flat and perfect.

When they finished, Nico put his pages face down on his knees. "The letter," he said.

"What about it?"

"You put it in the first scene. She seals it, she sets it right there on the bowl, the audience is going to watch it the whole time. And then it never comes back. Who's it to? What happens to it?"

Hannah said it was just something her mother had done that day, that she had put it in because it was true, and Nico said he got that, but the stage wasn't a kitchen, the stage was a machine, and anything you show that clearly, the audience will sit there waiting for it to matter. Kaiden looked at the tape outline of the counter and said, slowly, that there was actually a name for this. "Chekhov's gun," he said. "It's from the playwright Anton Chekhov. Anything clearly shown on stage early should matter later in the play."

Hannah stood very still, holding the script against her ribs. She had wanted the letter to be exactly what it had been in real life, a thing her mother did and never explained, sealed and abandoned, one more small lock on a door Hannah had stopped knocking on years ago. That was the honest version. But Kaiden and Nico were both watching the rectangle of tape as if the letter were sitting on it right now, recalcitrant, refusing to be part of the machine, and she understood that honesty on stage was not the same as inventory. The audience could not see her whole childhood. They could only see what she chose to show them, and every choice was a promise.

"Read the last page again," she said, and when Kaiden read it, she heard the ending differently: her mother taking the plate away, washing it, and Hannah had written nothing about the fruit bowl at all. In real life the letter had stayed there for three days and then disappeared, and Hannah had never asked, and her mother had never said, and the second time her brother came home from the station, the social worker had used the word recidivism in the hallway, quietly, as if the word itself might be heard through the door. Hannah had looked it up that night. She still couldn't decide whether the word had made the thing clearer or had just made it sound inevitable.

She sat down on a folding chair with the script and a pen. She could cut the letter, and the play would be clean, and something true would leave with it. Or she could keep it and make it fire, and that would be a lie, because nothing had come of that letter, not that day, not ever, as far as she knew. She crossed out a line, wrote another, crossed that out too, and recalibrated the whole shape of the ten minutes in her head, moving scenes like furniture, until Nico leaned over her shoulder and read what she had written: her mother picks up the envelope from the bowl, holds it, and puts it back down, unopened, unexplained.

"That's not an answer," Nico said.

"I know," Hannah said. She stood, taped a small square on the counter where the bowl would be, and said, "Places. From the top."

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: At a Passover Seder the youngest child present customarily asks the Four Questions from the Haggadah, beginning with 'Why is this night different from all other nights?'
story:
Brody had read the whole Haggadah cover to cover twice, which was why he wasn't nervous walking into the synagogue social hall with his mother. That was the story he'd told Kyla in the parking lot anyway, and he'd half believed it until he saw the tables.

The community Seder filled the hall with folding tables and paper cups of grape juice. Mr. Szabó stood at the head table arranging prayer books into straight lines, adjusting a microphone that wasn't turned on yet. He ran the evening like an autocrat, which Brody had heard his mother say with affection, moving candles two inches left, straightening a plate of parsley. At the far end, a cousin of Brody's, a senior in high school, was bent over a book with her little sister, drilling her the way you'd drill multiplication tables.

Kyla found him by the coat rack. "You said you knew all of it."

"I do know all of it." He had read the Haggadah twice. The problem was that reading was not remembering, and somewhere between the wise son and the wicked son the words had gone soft in his head. "It's fine."

"Then why do you keep checking your phone."

"My mom texted." She hadn't. The screen was dark.

His mother went to help in the kitchen, which she did every year, leaving Brody alone at a table of people he mostly knew by face. The little girl across from him was still whispering to her sister, and Brody caught the shape of what they were doing. She was the youngest kid in her family, and at a Passover Seder the youngest child present asked the Four Questions, the ones that started the whole telling. "Why is this night different from all other nights," she recited, stumbling over the second clause, and her sister corrected her, patient, like a coach running the same drill until the muscles learned it.

Then the sister's phone buzzed and she left for the hallway, and Mr. Szabó tapped the microphone, and it was time.

Except the little girl was crying. Quietly, the way kids cry when they've decided not to, her chin tucked down, her hands flat on the closed book. Her sister wasn't back. Mr. Szabó waited at the head table with the patience of a man who had run this evening for thirty years and would run it for thirty more.

Brody's fear wasn't abstract. It was somatic, a thing in his hands and throat, and telling himself he had read the book twice did nothing to it. He leaned across the table.

"You know the first line," he said. "I heard you."

"It went away," she said.

"It didn't. Just do the first line and the rest is in the book. The words are right there. You're not saying it from nothing."

She looked at the Haggadah, then at him.

"I'll say it with you," he said. "Quiet. Nobody'll hear me."

Mr. Szabó's voice came over the microphone. "We're ready for the questions."

Brody stood up with her. He hadn't planned to; his body did it, and afterward he would tell Kyla it had been a calculated decision. The little girl opened the book. "Why is this night different from all other nights?" Her voice shook on the first question and steadied by the second, and Brody said the words half a beat behind her, low enough that only she could hear, reading off the page because he did not, in fact, have them memorized. On the third question he lost his place and she pulled ahead of him. On the fourth she didn't need him at all.

When they sat down, people were smiling at them, and Mr. Szabó nodded once from the head table, which was apparently a decoration.

Kyla caught his sleeve. "You didn't know it."

"I knew the structure of it."

"Brody."

He exhaled. "I read it. I didn't learn it. There's a difference and I found out where it is."

She laughed into her napkin. He found a pen in his jacket and, while Mr. Szabó began the telling, Brody copied the Four Questions onto the inside of the tablecloth's paper covering, letter by letter, transcribing them the way you'd copy a phone number you refused to trust to memory. Then he tore off the strip, folded it, and slid it across the table to the little girl, who pocketed it without looking up from her grape juice.

Kyla leaned over. "You going to do that next year too?"

"Ask me next year," he said, and turned the page.

activity: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
knowledge_domain: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
fact: The principle is named after the French chemist Henry Louis Le Chatelier, who stated it in 1884.
story:
Alice had told herself she would not check the leaderboard again, but by Wednesday she had memorized its order anyway: Kim first, Alice second, and the gap between them a single percentage point that seemed to expand whenever she looked at it. The prize was a cheque for two hundred dollars and a line on a college application, and the quiz that would decide it covered equilibrium, which Ms. Das had promised would be on Friday's test in exactly the form Alice feared most: predict how a temperature change shifts a reaction, and defend the prediction.

"Explain it to me," Kim said at the lab bench, tapping the practice sheet with one pencil. "Heat on the left, heat on the right, I keep flipping them."

"You add heat, the system runs away from heat," Alice said, and then, because that wasn't really an answer, "The equilibrium shifts to absorb what you added." She could make it work on paper. What she couldn't do yet was say why it worked, and Ms. Das had a way of standing beside a desk in silence until why materialized.

Kim copied Alice's worked example in quick strokes and then didn't hand the sheet back. She held it. "My dad's meeting with the bank Thursday," she said, in a voice so level it had to be rehearsed. "If it goes badly, second semester might look different for me." She slid the paper across the bench and smiled. "Anyway. Friday."

That night Alice read the textbook chapter twice and understood it less each time, which felt almost malevolent, as though the chemistry were actively withholding itself. Somewhere past eleven she found the name in a footnote and stopped. Le Chatelier. She had been saying it in her head for two days without once asking whose it was.

The twist came, as twists do, in a fluorescent room. Their class had a field trip Thursday morning to the science museum, and while the others clustered around the liquid nitrogen demonstration, Alice drifted to a wall panel on industrial chemistry and found the name again, printed under a portrait of a bearded man with tired eyes. She took out her phone.

"Are you supposed to be on that?" Kim asked, appearing at her shoulder.

"Looking him up." Alice tilted the screen. "Henry Louis Le Chatelier. That's the full name. It says he was a French chemist." She scrolled. "And he stated the principle in 1884."

"Stated it. Like he didn't invent it, just said it out loud."

"Somebody had to say it first." Alice read the line again, and the phrase kept its exact shape in her mind, the way an equation does when you finally stop paraphrasing it. The system responds to oppose the change. Not resist, not undo. Oppose. It absorbed what you added, and what it absorbed, it kept, and the new equilibrium was not the old one restored. She stood there long enough that the demonstration crowd moved on without them.

Friday, Ms. Das set the quiz face down on each desk, and Alice read the last question first, the way she always did: an endothermic reaction at equilibrium, temperature increased, which way does it shift, justify. She wrote toward the products and then, instead of stopping, kept going, writing about a system that runs from what you force on it and settles somewhere new, and she could hear the sentence in Le Chatelier's borrowed voice. When she handed in the paper she saw Kim's hand hovering over her own final answer, pen still down, eraser already out.

They got their marks in the afternoon. Kim had missed one, a sign error, and had erased and re-erased the equilibrium question so many times the paper had gone thin and grey. Alice had missed none. On the leaderboard, the two names changed places, and Kim looked at it for a moment and then turned away, and Alice remembered the bank, and Thursday, and the way Kim had smiled while sliding the practice sheet across the bench.

"Hey," Alice said, catching her at the lockers. "Split it."

"Split what."

"The cheque. If it comes." Alice closed her locker and held her quiz against her chest. "You knew the chemistry. You just ran out of time running away from it."

Kim looked at her for a long second. "Ask Ms. Das if that's allowed."

activity: getting a first part-time job
knowledge_domain: getting a first part-time job
fact: Under US federal child labor rules, workers under 18 may not operate power-driven meat slicers, even in a grocery store deli or restaurant.
story:
Audrey arrived at the day camp cafeteria twenty minutes early, which she regretted immediately, because it gave her time to notice everything that could go wrong. The folding tables had been pushed against the wall for the staff meeting, and Ms. Fraser stood at the front with a clipboard, calling out assignments for the last week of the summer session. Audrey had spent two months as a junior counselor, unpaid, watching the paid staff leave with paychecks, and today Ms. Fraser was going to tell her whether the camp's kitchen vendor, the man who ran the sandwich cart by the lake, would take her on for the fall.

He would. That part went easily. After the meeting, Ms. Fraser pulled her aside by the drink coolers and said the vendor needed someone Saturdays and two afternoons a week, minimum wage, starting the weekend after camp ended. Audrey thanked her twice, which was one time too many, and walked out to the picnic tables to find Deshawn and Samira, who were hosing down the paddle boards.

"You got it?" Samira asked, turning the hose off.

"I got it."

Deshawn raised the scraper he'd been using on barnacles in a small salute. "First real money. What are you going to buy?"

"A winter coat," Audrey said, and meant it, though she was also already spending the rest of it in her head, on the deposit for the college trip in spring, on notebooks, on bus fare she wouldn't have to ask her mother for.

The Saturday she started, the vendor, a broad man with a paper hat, put her on the register first, then moved her to the back counter where the sandwiches were assembled. It was good work, repetitive in a way that let her think. He was fair about breaks and unfair about nothing. Halfway through the afternoon he looked at the line stretching toward the beach and said, "I need someone on the slicer. The deli order's behind." He pointed at the machine beside the prep sink, its circular blade still spinning down from the morning shift, and then at Audrey. "You're the closest. Just feed the turkey through and keep your fingers behind the guard."

She had her hand on the pusher handle before something in her went cold. "I can't," she said. "I'm sixteen. Under federal child labor rules, workers under eighteen can't operate power-driven meat slicers, even in a grocery store deli or a restaurant."

The vendor blinked. "Who told you that?"

"Nobody. I read it." She had, two nights before, in a fit of anxiety about the job, scrolling through the Department of Labor's youth employment page at her kitchen table while her mother watched television. She had thought it was trivia then, something to know and never use.

He looked at her for a long moment, and she braced for the argument, for the speech about how the guard made it safe, how everyone started somewhere. Instead he called across the kitchen to the other new hire, a lanky seventeen-year-old from the high school, and held up his hand before the boy reached the slicer. "Not you either. You're seventeen. Same rule." He turned back to Audrey, and the line kept growing, and the sandwich cart's reputation for fast service was quietly being adjudicated in real time at the register. "Okay," he said. "You do bread and condiments only. I'll slice."

Afterward, when the rush had died, he came and stood next to her at the sink. "Most kids your age wouldn't have said anything," he said. "They'd have just done it." He was not, she decided, an iconoclast; he was something better, a man who liked rules when someone could tell him what they were. He told her she could come back Saturday, and that if she was going to be this kind of worker, he'd teach her the ordering system too, which was a real skill, a bookkeeping skill, something that traveled.

She rode the bus home with her apron folded in her bag and her first day's pay in a sealed envelope, and she found she couldn't decide how to hold the afternoon in her mind. She had said no to her boss on her first shift, and it had cost him time and probably a few customers, and he had thanked her anyway. But she thought too of the seventeen-year-old, walking to the slicer without hesitation before he was stopped, of all the people who would have fed the turkey through and kept their fingers behind the guard and been fine. She didn't know whether she had been brave or only cautious with a regulation she'd happened to read. Both felt true at once, and she let them sit together.

At her stop, she got off and stood a moment in the heat of the late afternoon. Her mother's building was four blocks away, and between here and there was the thrift shop where the winter coats were, and she had enough now for one. She pushed through the door, and the bell rang above her, and the woman behind the counter looked up and said, "Back again?"

"Back again," Audrey said, and walked toward the racks.
